div.head: GIRL'S CASHMERE FROCK.
div.p: GIRL'S CASHMERE FROCK.

This is a pretty dress for a girl of about fif- teen years of age. A deep shade of old-roso cashmere is suggested for its realisation, though it could be carried out equally well in any fine woollen material. The bodice is cut with kimono over-sleeves, which are edged with fancy silk braid a little darker than the cashmere. The round opening at the neck is outlined with braid,

and finished in front with a large bow of soft rose-coloured silk. The line of braid over the shoulders is carried down the front of the skirt and round over the hem. The guimpe and sleeves are of old-t,ose silk, the guimpe and long cuffs being finely 'tucked. This would make a useful school dress, carried out in navy-blue serge, trimmed with black mohair braid, and supplied with a change of under-blouses--one of tartan silk and another of some pretty light- coloured washing material.

div.head: FILET NET.
div.p: THE FILET NET.

The large-meshed filet net in colours is form- ing more and more the chief material for blouses for all occasions and for the delightful long transparent coats worn over evening gowns. It is one of the attractive fashions which cannot be copied cheaply, so it is assured of a long life. The whole essence of this novelty in blouses, the Tatter points out, is the beautiful hand embroi- dery with which it is decked. Thick floss silk is darned into the net to suit the wearer's fancy and taste in colour, and naturally lends itself to beautiful effects. The pattern can be of the slightest, or massed in a bold design upon the shoulders or sleeves. The most satisfactory colours are all brown and green shades, as the coloured embroidery is so effective upon these backgrounds. But in all cases the net should match the skirt with which it is worn, the colour scheme of the decoration being arranged accord- ingly. The irregularity of the embroidery—each being done to suit the bodiceupon which it is put—quite prevents it ever becoming one of the overdone fads we are all so anxious to avoid, if such is possible. TO-DAT'S RECIPk.

SPANISH SHOUTCANE.—Three eggs, two ounces of butter, four ounces of castor sugar, eight ounces of flour, one gill of milk, half-teaspoonful of powdered cinnamon, one teaspoonful of baking powder. Mix together, and then sift the flour, baking powder, and cinnamon. Cream the butter, add the eggs and the sugar, and beat ontil very light. Stir in the dry ingredients, but do not knead the mixture for this kind of chqrteake. Bake in a shallow tin, and when done nave reaay a frosting made ot the beaten white of one egg, one tablespoonful of castor sugar, and a quarter. teaspoonful of powdered cinnamon. Spread this on top of tho cake, and return it to the oven until nicely browned.

div.head: ADAPTABILITY OF PRESENT-DAY STYLES.
div.p: ADAPTABILITY OF PRESENT-DAY STYLES.

With all the lavishness and exaggeration au present-day styles, -there never was a time when the woman who must consider the cost had more reason to take heart, for there is a picturesque- ness about gowns and wraps that is easily adapt- able for making over and readjusting, without the slightest fear of a result that will proclaim itself home-made, or a relic of last year propped up for continued service.

div.head: SMART CLOTH COSTUME.
div.p: SMART CLOTH COSTUME.

A deep plum-coloured cloth is used for this smart costume. The skirt has two pleats in front, and is trimmed with inch-wide mohair braid a little darker than the cloth. The bolero or bodice has a box-pleat down each side of the front, which is ornamented with some handsome buttons. Over the shoulders there is a wide strap'of the cloth, cut square across the front a few inches above the waist line. This is attached to the bolero at the inner edge only, which is

bordered with a plain line of braid, the outer edge being trimmed with braid and a very weal' ball fringe. Instead of revers. the nsek is finished with a band of Oriental embroidery. The deeves are arranged with a double box-pleat down the side, and finished with braid-trimmed cuffs.

div.head: WIRED COLLARS AND HEADACHES.
div.p: WIRED COLLARS AND HEADACHES.

There is an art in the wiring of high collars, declares a fashion writer. Certain veins in the neck carry up the blood to the brain. Preseure on these soon, produces headache, but very often the victim is entirely unaware of tho cause. Physiolozx is tile last subiect considered neces-

sttry in our schools, ana yet even a srignt knowledge of it would avert a considerable - amount of wifrorin.2: if. a way of &lan*. trig vie collar supports that, while attoraing all necessary aid to the collar, avoids pressure on the veins. But how many of our little dress- makers" have given the subject a thought? All they know is that nothing gives a gown a smarter look than a well-fitted, well-boned high lace or net collar. And they are right. It is one of the cases in which even the quality of the material matters less than the cut and fit. THE QUEEN'S JEWELS.

On such an occasion as the opening of Parlia- ment Queen Alexandra may be truly said to rifle her jewel-caskets, says the Sketch. On her head she wears the becoming crown of large dia- monds which would be so trying to many a royal lady, but which in the case of Queen Alex- andra is admirably adapted to set off the ex- treme regularity of her features. Her Majesty also wears a priceless lace veil, fastened to her hair by jewelled pins, which repeat and recall the lustre of her favourite jewels—namely. pearls. Indeed, it may be said that pearls play a predominant part in all the specially lovely parures of the Queen, and the , distinguishing feature of her costume at the opening of Parlia- ment is always magnificent *ropes of pearls, which reach from her Majesty's neck almost to the hem of her beautiful dress. The opening of Parliament is one of the few occasions which sees the Queen wear the Koh-i-Noor in public; and the broad ribbon of the Garter is held ia place by large brilliants and flat pearl brooches, as well as by numerous family" and other Royal Orders.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday February 8, 1908.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday February 8, 1908.
THE CELEBRITY.
[ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
DY WARWICK PEEPING, , Author of "Love Among the Ruins," " Uther and Ingrains," &c.

Percival Potter, Esq., author and critic, had rented a cottage for the summer at Heatherden. umid the purple of the Wessex- hills. Percival Potter was a distinguished man, one of the elect who kept the gates of literature—praised or con- temned; more often the latter. He it was who wrote those brilliant and slashing articles for the Daily Dromedary, articles intended to educate the public in the matter of literary taste. Mr. Potter , was a caustic person. He tilted his thin penetrat- ing nose at creation, surveyed the universe patronisingly through his pince-nez, and delivered leeretals on all such matters as came beneath his ; aimble and superficial notice. Heatherden was an unsophisticated village. Hence it had greeted Mr. Potter's advent with a , thrill of curiosity and pleasure. Nor was Mr. Percival Potter unprepared to patronise such rustic votaries as brought garlands to lay before the feet of Literature. That summer the celebrity was a frequent guest at the Heatherden garden ; parties and functions of the kind—Mr. Potter ; was not adverse to parading his abilities before , the social Perditas of the place:. Miss Pamela Canyon was a young woman with a great love for literature and the usual feminine propensity for idolising "Literary stars." More- over, Miss Pamela was a very comely young damsel, with her dream-filled eyes, her pale face and small, mobile mouth. She had consumed novels by the score, and poetry flowed like a perpetual brook through her young brain. Nor was she a mere feeder on fiction in the superficial sense. Like many an intelligent and well-read womar% she had that natural selecting power, that elemental critical instinct that discovers the true from the false. When Miss Pamela was introduced to Percival Petter, Esq., at the Vicarage garden-party, she flattered herself that the critic of the Daily Dromedary was a man worthy of her serious respect. Heatherden was not an intellectual centre. Miss Pamela had often lamented in secret that there wore so few folk to whom she could confide her ideals. She had been compelled to dream her dreams in silence, to enjoy her inner life in the solitude of her own home. Even the Colonel her father was an austere and stiff- backed patriarch who read the Times from page to page, and admired nothing so much as the practical. Her feminine friends in the neigh- bourhood had not advanced on Emma Jane Wor- boise and Mrs. Henry Wood. They were beauti- fully innocent of all modern thought, and were exceedingly amiable though they were not learned. The first remark Mr. Potter made to Miss Pamela concerning a subject that was of interest to thorn both ran much as follows:
"Do you give any attention, Miss Canyon, to the ephemeral filagree work of modern literature ? "
Mr. Percival Potter always delivered himself of his cleverness with a certain idle hauteur, complacent yet semi-scornful loftiness, as though he had culled all wisdom and found it dust.

"I read a good deal," was the girl's retort. Percival Potter tilted his yellow face to the sun, peered at Miss Pamela slantwise from his beglassed grey eyes, and pursed up his prim and lipless mouth. 'Fiction ?" he asked. "Regularly." "What else, if I may inquire ?" "Essayists—Emerson, for instance." "Poor old platitudinarian ! Let me warn you, Miss Canyon, against Emerson."

Mr. Potter appeared to be a man of bold con- victions. Pamela experienced a sense of shamed surprise. The critic doubtless thought her very provincial, since she. had been duped into believing in Emerson as a thinker.
"I adlire Dickens greatly," she said, by way of creating a diversion, gravitating from intellect to heart.

Mr. Potter's grey eves scanned her again with a certain scientific pity. A suspicious smile over- spread his self-assertive countenance. "Superstition dies hard," he observed. "You do not believe in Dickens ?"

"My dear Miss Carlyon, the younger and more enlightened spirits of the day have come to regard Dickens as a paltry sentimentalist. He was no thin ker, and had no style. He was vulgarly religious and emotional to a degree. His eternal gush would sicken most cultured folk of the day. Dickens is dead in a double sense. Have you ever read Tufter, the coming man ?" Miss Pamela appeared bemused. Such rending of classical foundations toppled her idols from pillar and from arch. She blushed a little and confessed her ignorance. "Tufter ? No, I am afraid P have never heard of him."

Mr. Potter refrained from reproof; his face was a study of divine pity. "Read him, Miss Canyon," he said, emphati- cally; "no one can be considered cultured who has not read Tufter's poems. He has genius, real genius. I was one of the first to detect his promise. By the way, have you read my book on the Minor Poets ? " Again Miss Pamela blushed. "I will get it at once," she said; "I am sure it will delight me." Percival Potter was convinced that afternoon that he had established an empire in Miss Pamela's heart. The critic was not a handsome man physically. His shanks were long and limp, and weak at the knees. His somewhat profuse hair haloed a thin and irritable face. His shoulders sloped precipitously—his whole frame betrayed that fireless intellectuality begotten of a sedentary life. Though a veritable Samson in the matter of his hair, a sturdy public school fifth former could have broken the critic over his knee. _

- Mr. Percival Potter made it his especial business to see much of Miss Canyon those summer months. The girl had money and a pretty face. Mr. Potter orated while Pamela listened. With the supreme conceit that characterised his literary articles, he instructed his disciple in the virtues and vices of English literature. She had read Tufter's poems and had failed to understand them, save that her fresh young heart revolted from a certain cynical eroticism that pervaded the pages. She had also toiled through Mr. Potter's Minor Poets, and had discovered that the work consisted mainly of a Potterian monologue on the Potterian idiosyn- crasies. "You do not play tennis ? " said Miss Pamela, as she reverted to the celebrity one August after- noon in the Vicarage garden. Mr. Potter yawned. "I am afraid lam too much in earnest to be solaced by sport. Exercise bores me."

"And yet some of our modern tetheticists declare art to be play." "A self-assertive theory, Miss Canyon, nothing more; a mere physiological dogma. People are too proud of their own principles. It is a pre- sumptuous ago." Pamela regarded him with the mild reverence of youth. "The responsibilities of a critic must be very heavy," she said. For the moment, Mr. Potter seemed to suspect banter. He was not a man who could tolerate playful sarcasm. He eyed the girl through his powerful glasses, but she appev •ed innocent as a white rose.

"We are the doorkeepers of Fame," he observed; "it is our duty to beat back rash and conceited people, who are intoxicated by egotism and imagine themselves clever." "True literary power is rare, I suppose ? " Mr. Potter bent his Jovian brows, and appeared to consider the remark with critical severity. "I have only come across two good books in a year," he said. "Then you have to condemn many ? " , Mr. Potter smiled assent. It was his usual habit to attack works of any weight and promise, and to praise books which he had no cause to fear. There was no peril in praising trash, whereas he had a serious reason for belittling merit.

"But you try to help beginners," said Miss Pamela, with an appealing smile. "My dear Miss Canyon," was the retort, "we are critics, not literary philanthropists." There was one man in Heatherden, however, who had failed to bow the knee to the Zeus of the Daily Dromedary. That man was the Rev. John Masters, curate and Christian. Creed or no creed, the clergyman hated the celebrity with a wholeheartedness that was perfectly logical. "Honest Jack," as the villagers called him, had been the avowed esquire of Miss Pamela Carlyon. He was a sturdy young man, virile, frank, and open-hearted, a man such as Charles Kingsley wnald have lovell. He as no mere crow : rather, a layman in clerical guise. At all events, he was human enough to nurture a strenuous hatred bad contempt for Mr, Percival Potter, _

The curate and L'ameln, Canyon had been very good friends till the celebrity had appeared within the bounds of Heatherden. Percival Potter had sneered John Masters from the field, had repulsed him actually by the supreme offensiveness of his patronage. The egregious and vapid vanity of the young critic had kindled fires of wrath in Jack Masters' heart. The curate was slow with his tongue, too honest and sincere to engage Mr. Potter in verbal subtleties. Moreover; he had been calmly snubbed by Miss Pamela when he had ventured to express a private opinion a Mr. Potter's capabilities as a critic. , John Masters was not the man to thrust himself forward when his presence appeared to be an encumbrance to Miss Pamela's enjoyment. Hence, Mr. Potter had been able to monopolise Miss Carlyon's attention. And perhaps, being a woman, she was a little flattered by the distinction the celebrity's friendship conferred upon her. John Masters had been playing tennis, watch- ing the while Miss Pamela and Mr. Potter chatting together under a chestnut tree. The celebrity hid the light of his countenance prema- turely that afternoon, pleading work and letters in excuse. John Masters, ruddy and boyish, ventured to take the celebrity's place. Miss Pamela received him with a smile that suggested. patronage. She had liked John Masters more perhaps than she had realised. Mr. Percival Potter's splendour had dulled calmer intelleets and warmer hearts for the moment. "So the critic has fled ? " "You do not like Mr. Potter, Jack.'

The curate smiled a peculiar smile, tightened up his mouth, and tilted his chin. He would have given much to have had an unclerical combat with the celebrity in a quiet corner of the churchyard. Mr. John Masters' fist itched incontinently to plant itself on the bridge of Mr. Potter's thin and contemptuous nose...
"Mr. Potter is a celebrity," was the curate's retort. "Heaven forbid that I should blaspheme against the critic of the Daily Dromedary!"

Miss - Pamela's upper lip lifted at the angles. "I am afraid you do not appreciate him," she said. "I •admire Mr. Potter—at a distance." "He is a Most striking man." "Evidently so, Miss Canyon. At college we should have treated him with distinction."

"An honorary degree ? " "I referred to the nearest cow-pond." Miss Pamela conceived herself offended, nor was she slow in confessing her sentiments. "It is a strange thing," she said, "how a clever r.an always arouses jealousy in others." John Masters coloured liked like a schoolboy. "Your really great man does not pose.perpetually as a genius," he retorted. "Mr.. Potter does not rose:"

"Perhaps not consciously." Miss Pamela lost patience. "Jack, you are:an absolute cynic. Oblige me by refraining from referring to Mr. Potter in the future." "Certainly," retorted the curate, with a still little bow. 'I had formed my own conclusions. I assure you my motives were mainly dis- interested.' "Disinterested indeed!"

"I only desired to warn you against trusting in a prig and an egotist. I think we had better drop the subject. Please forgive me if I have hurt your feelings." "Oh! they are not worth considering," said the girl, with a flash of the eye. Miss Pamela Canyon was possessed of a secret which she had confided to no one, not even to her father the Colonel. Miss Pamela had money of her own, and also a poetical impulsiveness that had driven her to arrange for the anonymous publication of certain of her poems. The village was utterly ignorant of Miss Carlyon's poetical longings. "Rose Leaves" was the title inscribed upon the volume. Miss Pamela had adopted the name of Gabriel Grandison. The poems were to appear early in the autumn, before the general flood of fiction and of verse. Miss Pamela revelled in the anonymous with true feminine zest. She had concealed her poetical proclivities with consummate skill. Not that she feared for the impression her book would make. Above other amiable vanities, she had a jealous belief in her own power, and in the strength of her opinions. She did not doubt of being hailed with enthusiasm as a new and ardent torch in a dead and ashy age. .

Her one great temptation that summer had been to confess her venture to Mr. Percival Potter, and to invoke his aid. Pamela's sincerity had triumphed, however, and she had suppressed such leanings towards premature publicity. She would wait for Mr. Potter's unbiassed and honest verdict; nor did she doubt that he would hail "Hose Leaves" as a work of art. _

Thus it befel that September season that Mr. Percival Potter received a consignment of books fer "reviewing," Miss Pamela's among them. The critic was thirsting for some innocent author upon whom he might swoop and flesh his talons. The season was a dull one. Mr. Potter needed material for a caustic and scintillating article, and "Rose Leaves" fell to him at the opportune moment. He smiled one of his metaphysical, self-assertive smiles, and opened the flood-gates of his scorn on Gabriel Grandison's head. The following evening he met Miss Pamela on the Heatherden moors. She was wandering home from a neighbouring village, radiant with the rhythm of her own songs in her heart. For days she had been dreaming of this book of hers, with its mystical tone, its quaint wood - cuts, its emblazoned cover. Her vanity was innocent enough, sheer joy in this fairy child begotten of her own brain. Her heart was full of the gold of the sunset. She had been singing as she crossed the moors.

Mr. Percival Potter regarded her with critical approval that eve Ling, as he ambled at her side, weak-kneed and shoulderless. He was gloating in thought over a certain brilliant and coruscat- ing article that ho had posted to the Daily Dromedary on "A New Volume of Verse." Mr. Potter had indulged in splendid sarcasm, in Olympic scorn. He felt particularly pleased with the powerful passes of his pen. They grew confidential these two that Septem- ber evening. Mr. Potter's tongue waxed sug- gestive. His grey eyes were amatory behind his pince-nez. He talked for effect; was in excellent humour.

"Life is a glorious thing," he observed, senti- meotally,"when youth meets youth. What poetry there is in yonder sky, what imagery in yonder woods! Nature, Miss Canyon, I adore Nature from the bottom of my heart." "It is so restful," said the girl; "so calm, so sublime."

"Yes, when one finds a sympathetic soul to share one's own enthusiasm. " Mr. Potter pondered. Miss Canyon had money and a pretty face. The celebrity was debating with himself the advantages and disadvantages of the matrimonial state. They had neared Heatherden. The church spire streaked the azure; the river shimmered through the meadows. "It is good to talk to a man who understands," said Miss Pamela, with her face aglow. "Ah! you are too kind," retorted the celebrity, with a sentimental smirk.
"I approciate all the sympathy you ham shown to me.

"My dear Miss Pamela, it is I who lam grate- ful. The debt is on my shoulders." Mr. Potter's shoulders were narrow enough.— narrow as his egotism—but he could pretend to chivalry. The pair parted at the end of the village. Miss Inmela's hand remained clasped for some moments in Mr. Potter's bony claw. He smiled at her unutterable things, but witheld his confessions for a season. His vanity whim- pered as he stalked homewards towards his cottage. The girl was quite bearable; had dis- crimination enough to appreciate his genius. Two mornings later, Miss Pamela Canyon sat over the breakfast-table with the Daily Dromedary unfolded in her quivering hands. She was white to the lips with mingled anger and distress. Her eyes ran on from line to line, growing more strained and bright us the words flowed past. The sensitive idealism of her woman's nature seemed smitten down and shamed by the flippant gibes, tho dishonest insinuations. Pamela was stunned mentally for the Moment. She threw the paper aside, moved to t window _seat, and sat and stared into the sunlit garden. Mr. Percival Potter's critique ran much as fellows:

"If imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, then Mr. Gabriel Grandison may be dubbed a literary sycophant in the severest sense. We would not advise him to filch his material and his imagery from William Morris and Rossetti. Mr. Grandison is obviously a very young man. Let him in the future eschew petticoat poetry. We do not charge him outright with deliberate plagiarism. but we do warn Mr. Grandison that I,,myue ranxeu ny the uncharitable rritli tiler t.
"'Rose Leaves '—a significant title, seeing that there is much leafy verbiage in the book and but little bloom—pretends to be a collection ol

poems compiled in idie moments for the author's personal delectation. Firstly, we would advise Mr. Grandison to devote his idle moments to potato growing or wood carving. Mr. Grandison is not even a versifier. As for poetry, his pre- tences are purely ridiceous. When he writes passably, which is rarely, he is obviously copy- ing those who have gone before him. Only when he writes badly, and that is often, can he be considered to be displaying his gifts or misgifts in his verse."

After some such prologue, Mr. Potter pro- ceeded after the most approved methods of malicious criticism to treat with transcendant scorn the various prime poems from Miss Pamela's pen. He dubbed originality affecta- tion, condemned the fanciful and the imaginative as artificial. He pretended to regard pathos as hysterical sentimentalism, passion as sexuality veiled in coloured phrases. There was a quip at every turn, a gibe in every sentenoe. No doubt the critique was seintillant enough, but like many such productions it was utterly scandalous in the matter of morality. Mr. Potter's purpose was to coruscate at the expense of the poet. His sneers were "to the gallery," his epigrams for the tickling of his own conceit. As for poor Pamela, she sat at the open window looking out upon the garden, with the morning breezes playing upon her burning cheeks. Even authors are human, and expect some courtesy from the hirelings of the pen. Pamela, being a woman, was the more sensitive to such methods of attack. The critique with the pert P.P. at the end thereof had shrivelled her for the moment even as a north wind shrivels a rose. The fact that Percival Potter's article was both dishonest and dishonourable did not weigh with her for the moment. She was too cast down, too shamed to conceive herself justified by the positive merits her work possessed. This mood of dejection, however, was not for long. She was a girl with no mean amount of spirit, and as the realisation of the malignity of the attack increased within her mind, so her anger kindled and grew apace. Percival Potter indeed! Who was Mr. Potter that lie should assume such authority in the matter of criticism ? He was a young man, and a very ambitious one, jealous, as she had more than once suspected, of seeing the coronet of success on any foreign brow. The illusion passed in a moment; she saw Percival Potter as he was. How had she been so blind to his preposterous vanity, his over- powering egotism ? She remembered his vapour- ings, his thin and consequential voice, his profuse hair, his utter lack of honest virility. The vision of Jack Masters, strong and boyish, generous and open-hearted, sped athwart her vision. After all, Jack Masters was a man. He did not pretend to patronise creation. Nor had he ever referred to Dickens as "a snivelling sentimentalist." When Mr. Potter ambled up to Miss Pamela that day in the Heatherden meadows' his smirks were chilled by such a frost that he gaped in astonishment and wiped his glasses. The celebrity was amazed, baffled. His glibness forsook him; his ingenuity was repulsed by the girl's pale face and contemptuous eyes. His confessions were petrified upon his tongue. Yet be it known Mr. Potter's vanity suffered more severely than his heart. He watched the Sappho of Heatherden playing tennis that afternoon with Jack Masters, and comforted himself with a complacent sneer, and an epigram that celebrated the notorious falsity of the feminine heart. None the less the situation was explained to him in later years when he discovered the identity of Gabriel Grandison, when Mrs. John Masters' poetry had been "foisted into notoriety by the crass sentimentalism of the British public," [THE END.]

div.head: RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
Proposed Slaughter House.
A PROTEST.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at Bewsey Chambers on Wednesday, Dr. Murray presiding. There were also present : Messrs. A. Brooks, G. Mather, W. Furness, R. Forsberg, W. Stenier, P. Longton, J. Backhouse, J. Ball, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), F. W. Kerfoot (inspector), and Dr. Sephton (medical officer).
TIIE PROPOSED SLAUGHTER-ROUSE.
A PROTEST.

A letter was read from Rev. G. Vale Owen stating that he should be glad if the Clerk would draw the attention of the Council to the following protest : " Hearing that plans are in preparation and that leave to erect a slaughter-house on land near Orford New Church is about to be asked, we as sidemen, church officers and Sunday School teachers in connection with the church beg leave respectfully to enter a most urgent protest against the erection of such a building in proximity to the new church and to the site of the vicarage which is shortly to be erected. We take this step with full conviction that if a slaughterhouse is allowed to be erected on such a spot it will be a source of great annoyance to to the parishioners." The protest was signed by various workers connected with the new church.

Mr. BROOKS said the slaughter-house would be 180 yards from the church and 80 yards from the road. He thought it was a ridiculous protest. The CLERK was instructed to write to the Rev. O. Vale Owen and inform him that the Council had no power to interfere.

div.head: LONGFORD HOTEL.
div.p: LONGFORD HOTEL.

A letter was reaciii:OM-ilesSi;:-oreenall, Whitley and Company stating that about six months ago they repaired at a cost of about £lO a paving in front of the Longford Hotel ; subsequent to which the Surveyor to the Council re-formed the footpath higher than the level of their paving, and the water in consequence of that lodged on their land and caused a nuisance. They thought it only reasonable to ask if the Council would meet them in the cost of taking up their paving again and bringing it up to the Surveyor's level. Mr. NF,WCOMBIL suggested that the Council take no responsibility whatever, and the Clerk was instructed to write in accordance with that statement.

div.head: RINTON AND WARBURTON BRIDGE.
div.p: RINTON AND WARBURTON BRIDGE.

A letter was read from the Ship Canal Company with reference to the above bridge regretting that the sug- gestion made jointly by the Warrington Rural District Council and Bucklow Rural District Council that the two authorities should take over the bridge and the rotds leading thereto on terms to be arranged between the Councils and the Manchester Ship Canal Company, has been allowed to remain quiesce .t for so long, as it appeared to be the only reasonable solution of the difficulty connected with the matter.
The CLERK was instructed to write to the Bucklow Council and ask their view on the matter.

LIGHTING A.T A protest was sent in signed by several residents at Wiuwick complaining of the insufficiency of lamps and asking the Council to provide more lamps as 300 yards was lighted by one lamp only. Mr. MATHER said a committee was appointed to do the work, and he thought they had done it to the best of their abilities.
The protest was reforred to the Winwick Parish Council.

div.head: National Association of Prudential Assurance. Agents.
div.p: National Association of Prudential Assurance. Agents.

lln connecti—on with the local Branch of the above unity a most successful social gathering was held at the Winrrarleigh Café on Thursday evening last, when over 60 persons sat down to tea, which was fully appreciated, the catering being everything that could be desired. After tea the President (Mr. J. Darbyshire), opened the programme with a few well- chosen remarks,congratulating the local union upon the success of the first year's work,it being in a very healthy 1 and progressive condition. The main feature of its ' propaganda is for mutual help and education on matters conceining insurance. Songs were given by Mr. J. Leech " Queen of the Earth," ; Mr. E. Whitehouse, "Blow thou thy winter wind " ; Miss Mann," On the banks of Allan Water" ; Mr. ,J. Darbyshire, " My old Dutch." The humorous element was supplied by Mr. Newbold, who sang " What a mouth," creating much amusement; Mr. J. T. Rowland was at his best in two comic songs "Strawberries and cream" and " They're all fine girls ; also Mr. T. Brookes in two comic songs. The duets, " Excelsior" by Mr. A. Baker and Mr. e. Whitehouse ; "Larboard Watch " by Mr. and Mrs. Groom, and "Life's dream is o'er " by Miss Mann and Mr. Melbourne were of the highest order. Mr. Norman created much laughter by his funny read- ings entitled " John Booth and the Vicar " and a " Respectable Mon" ; recitations were given in grand 'style by Mr. G. Whitfield, " Moses mother-in-law " and " The Stuffed Monkey " ; Mrs. Melbourne gave "My bonnet " and Mr. Mann also recited. Instru- mental items were efficiently provided by Mr. Newbold ou the mandoline, and piano by Miss Green, who was also a very able accompanist.-- Mr. J. T. Rowlands, the district superintendent, in a brief but vigorous speech,spoke of the eicellent work done in the Warring- ton district during his term of office, and urged the agents to continue the good results.—The usual votes of thanks and singing of "Auld I.ang Syne " con- cluded a most enjoyable gathering. •

div.head: LAWSON CONTRACT.
div.p: THE LAWSON CONTRACT.
RECOGNITION OF COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON'S WORK.
Lively Discussion.

At the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening Alderman FORSHAW moved That a copy of the whole of the proceedings with reference to Lawson's contract, inquiry and areitration, be pre- sented to Councillor Pemberton as a slight recognition of the great interest he took in the matter." The Alderman said he thought the Council would agree with him when he said that Councillor Pemberton did take a very active interest in the matter, and it would be a courteous, as well as a generous, act on the part of the Council to present him with a copy of the proceedings as stated in the motion. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Pi E RPOINT seconded. '

Alderman BURTON thought it would be better for extracts to be taken out of the proceedings and each member of the Council to be supplied with a copy. Councillor SroTr asked what the cost of the volume would be.
_ The MAYon : There is no necessity for any printing to be done.

The Tows CLF.RY : I take it that I shall have to give him copies of all the papers I have in my possession. Councillor STOTT said he thought other members of the Council would like a copy of the proceedings ; he certainly would. Perhaps the Alderman would with- draw his motion so that copies could be sent to the members of the Council. He did not object to Coun- cillor Pemberton receiving a copy. The DEPUTY-MAYOR said that as chairman of the first inquiry committee he was as mush entitled to a copy as anyone, but he did not think it was worth the expense. It would only be filling a library with useless literature. (Laughter.) Councillor LORD said he understood several copies were printed while the arbitration proceedings were in progress and were not all used. He supposed there were one or two copies left. He thought Councillor Pember- ton was entitled to a spare copy considering the energy he had thrown into the matter.

Alderman EVAN', said a lurry would be required to take all the proceedings away. There were enough papers to fill a cottage. (Laughter.) The TOWN CLERK produced a large bound volume of the proceedings relating to the contract and said he had two additional copies, one of which he wished to send to the Museum.

Councillor BARTON said he had iio objection to Councillor Pemberton receiving the volume, and per- sonally, as a member of the committee, he {Councillor Barton) would be satisfied with the papers he already had in his. possession... . . .

COUnCillOr STBEL said that when he read the proposi- tion he did not know whether to weep or smile or fall on Councillor Pemberton's neck and say "Oh ! thou great benefactor." (Laughter.) He could not for the life of him understand why Alderman Forshaw should go out of his way to make such a proposition as that he had just submitted. Why should Councillor Pemberton receive a copy of the proceedings any more than other members of the Water Committee or the Corporotion ? It seemed to him that what was proposed was an insult to the other members of the committee. They might be about to confer the freedom of the borough on Councillor Pemberton, judging from the motion, which he should oppose. It seemed to him to be ridiculous to bring such a 'motion forward. They looked to the aldermen for words of wisdom, but he was afraid that Alderman Forshaw was wanting in wisdom in bringing forward the proposition. The motion was wanting in tact because other members of the committee must feel " Why has Councillor Pemberton been singled out in this way ? " If they passed the resolution it would be saying that Councillor Pemberton, and he alone, had brought the present great victory about. He did not think Councillor Pemberton would desire to take all the credit. Other members of the committee had done an equal share in carrying the matter through. Alder- man Evans went uo London and was present at the arbitration proceedings. Why should not he or the Mayor have a copy? Alderman FORSHAW : No one objects to it. Councillor STEEL : But you do. You single out Councillor Pemberton. . _

Alderman FORSHAW : Ido no such thing. I don't object to it at, all. Councillor STEEL : The whole thing, to my mind, is I absurd, and I am surprised that a member of the C ouncil of the standing of Alderman Forshaw, and a man of his years and experience, should have been so small-minded as to bring forward such a proposition. Alderman Fousuew : I can quite understand that to your mind it would be as you say. Councillor STEEL: I object to any personal insinua- tions

Alderman PIERPOINT said that, as he seconded the motion' it was only right that he should attempt to justify the position he had taken up. No doubt Coun- cillor Steel had a great deal of natural ability, and he had a great admiration for him, but the young rushed in where the aged feared to steal. (Laughter.) The reason he had for seconding the motion was that Coun- cillor Pemberton of all men in Warrington was respon- sible for the agitation that led up to the Investigation Committee. (dear, hear and applause.) His action on the committee, jointly with the °Sher members, was such that he insisted upon a certain line of procedure being followed—that Mr. Garside should be appointed as the engineer of the Corporation to guide them in the matter. He (Alderman Pierpoint) was now identifying himself with the Non-Trading Party. He did not know what he was according to some people— (laughter)—at all events he desired to identify himself as closely as he could with the Non-trading Party of the borough. Had it not been for their agitation which called for the formation of the Investigation Com- mittee, he did not hesitate to say—although at the time the preliminary investigation took place they were twitted about it—that the Corporation or the Water Committee would have considered very strongly whether they should take any action against Mr. Lawson. They were prepared to accede to the payment of a sum —at least report said that. (Cries of "Oh " and laughter.) Prominent officials of the Corporation were of opinion that no case lay and that they, as a Corporation, would have to pay a something but Councillor Pemberton had been the means of pushing the Corporation into the posi- tion of going to arbitration, and the result of that arbitration had been a signal victory. He (the speaker) did not know that he should have selected Alderman Forshaw's form of recognition. He should like to honour Councillor Pemberton in some way, but surely Alderman Forshaw was justified in say- ' that some mark of approbation should be accorded to Councillor Pemberton. There were three copies of the proceedings. One was to be kept at the Town Hall for inspection, he took it, by any member of the Council or any ratepayer, and one was very properly to be sent to the Museum ; therefore one copy was left. He (Alderman Pierpoint) did not care what was done with it, but he did not like these attempts to belittle Coun- cillor Penaberton after what he had done. (Haar, hear.) He had done more for the settlement of the matter than any other member of the Corporation. He did not like his way of proceeding at times, but he admired the honesty and persistency of his methods. In no action of his had he tried to advance his private interests, but he (Aldermad Pierpoint) would tell the Council what was attempted. What did they do? What did they tax him with ? Why did a large number of members of the Council look on and laugh while he was brought before an informal tribunal in the Town Hall ? They all expected he would be proved guilty of infamous conduct. Was he? No. He came out with flying colours, and no one could say he had done any. thing wrong in connection with his work in the Corporation, and it was, therefore,unmanly and improper to try to belittle his character. (Applause.) Councillor SINGLETON thought Mr. peas was as much to be praised as anyone. (Hear, hear.) If a copy of the proceedings was to be presented to Councillor Pemberton, Mr. Dem ought to have one also. Councillor ROGERS asked what the cost would be to give copies to all the members. The Towx CLERK : At a very moderate estimate,£l.oo. Councillor ASHCROFT contended that the Water Com- mittee had had very little to do with the matter. It was the Investigation Committee which forced the matter on. _

Councillor WILKINSON said it was the Investi- gation Committee that he was puzzled about. There was a committee formed to investigate the Lawson contract, and considering that that com- mittee never issued a report of its proceedings he could not see that it had much to do with the result. CONGRATULATIONS ON THE AWARD. At a meeting of the Water Committee the Town Clerk submitted the award made by the arbitrator, Mr. George Hill,in the arbitration proceedings between Mr. George Lawson and the Corporation. It was resolved,

that the Town Clerk be authorised to take such steps as he may consider necessary in order to enforce the award, and that the committee place on record their great satisfaction both with the result of the arbitra- - tion and the efficient and able manner in which all the proceedings have been conducted.

Aldernaan EVANS, in proposing the adoption of the minutes, said he thought they were all agreed that the arbitration proceedings had ended satisfactorily. He attended the proceedings in London, and the way in which the information was forthcoming was marvellous. There was not a fact stated but what could be proved or any question asked, but what could be answered with the greatest readiness ; and on many occasions counsel complimented the two staffs on the way the case had been got up. Compliments also flowed from the other side. It was due to Mr. Garside, of Ashton-under-Lyne, that his name should be included in the resolution— (hear, hear)—for the clear manner in which he placed the case before the arbitrator, which helped in a great measure to secure the verdict.

Alderman BOLTON, in seconding, expressed great satis- faction with the result. They could not have a better ending, and the officials had done their duty well. Especially did Mr. Carside deserve to be included in the resolution. (Hear, hear.) He (Alderman Bolton) was glad the case was finished with, after all the investigations which had taken taken place. Councillor PEMBERTON associated himself with the remarks of the proposer and seconder. There was no doubt Mr. Garside thoroughly investigated the matter, and the manner in which he went into it surprised even the members of the conimittee. He (Councillor Pem- berton) was in London during the arbitration proceed- ings, and the Deputy Town Clerk (Jr. Hallaway) and the Deputy Water Engineer (Mr. Gray) worked admir- ably. The whole case was conducted admirably, and every point raised by the opposition was answered immediately. They even gave the other side informa- tion and charts, and then whacked them. (Laughter.) All the departments concerned deserved great credit, ' and their excellent leading counsel, Mr. Hudson,worked in a way he had never seen counsel work before. He frequently stayed up until one and two o'clock in the morning so get up the case. The MAYOR said they might all congratulate them- selves and pat themselves on the back—(laughter)— but where there was a good leader the fight was always carried to a successful issue. In this case their Town Clerk had been a good leader in fighting the case— (hear, hear)—and he had capital men under him, and they all deserved their best thanks. (Hear, hear.) Alderman PIERPOINT said is was pleasing after they had passed through such a disagreeable time and all the difficulties had been swept away, to be able to co n- gratulate those who had had the work in hand. He spoke in praise of the members of the Water Com- mittee, Councillor Pemberton, and Mr. Garsid e. He was struck with the admirable way in which the case was conducted in all its details, not only by counsel, but the Town Clerk, the Deputy Town Clerk, Mr. Deas, and Mr. Gray, whose efforts were invaluable. They deserved the recognition of the Council, and the rate- payers collectively. The otficials concerned should have their holidays doubled. (Laughter.) The minutes were carried.

Funeral of Dutton Workhouse Master. On Monday afternoon the funeral took place at Overton Church, Frodsham, of the late Mr. Joseph Cunnah, master of the Dutton Workhouse of Runcorn Union, win died on the previous Thursday, after a brief illness. He was aged fifty-two years. He com- pleted twenty-one years' service as master in Novem- ber and his demise created wide regret. As the coffin was borne from the house the inmates lined up and uncovered. The cortege was met at Frodsham by a large number of guardians and officials and residents frun the surrounding district, including Mr. T. Baxter, C. C., chairman of the guardians ; Mr. Joseph Spruce, vice-chairman ; Mr. George Pilling, J.P., chairman of the Rural Council •, Mr. T. Wright, vice-chairman ; Alderman Norman, J.P., and Mr. J. F. Awbery, of Warrington Workhouse, representing the Workhouse Masters' As.sociation. The chief mourners were the widow and her Comm and two daughters, the officials of the workhouse, and the Rev. A. L. Temple, vicar cf Little Leigh, chaplain.
ROYAL COURT THEATRE, LIVERPOOL. A RECORD-BREAKING PANTONMIE.

Mr. Robert Arthur's twelfth Liverpool pantomime, "Cinderella," is still being played to crowded audiences despite the fact that nine performances a week are being given, and that we are now in " faieFebruary's month." This, of course, means that all records have been broken in fact, past pantomime successes at the Court Theatre are forgotten in the extraordinary popularity of the present production which, of course, has the famous Scottish comedian, Mr. Harry Lauder, as chief magnet. This week he has introduced a new song named, with that degree of amusing correctness that playgoers will realise the full meaning of when they hear it, " Sound Advice." The song is one of the best Mr. Lauder has ever delighted in rendering, and it creates roars of laughter at every performance, while the " advice," though amusing, is nevertheless " sound." Miss Langtyre, who has made such a pronounced success as the Prince, has also a new ballad, entitled "If your hair were not so curly," whilst Miss Meg Hamilton, the frolicsome Dandini, sings now, with infinite zest and some very clever chorus effects, " I'll tell Tilly on the Telephone." The superb character of the scenery remains the wonder of all beholders.

div.head: D G ATE SCHOOLS.
div.p: D G ATE SCHOOLS.

At a meeting of the Cottage Homes Committee, the resignation of the chaplain (Rev. W. Pollock Hill) who is leaving the district, was accepted, and the Committee placed on record their appreciation of the diligence and close personal attention to religious instruction shown by him during his connection with the Homes. The minutes were adopted on the proposition of Mr MATHER, seconded by Mrs. SIMPSON. MEDICAL APPOINTMEETS. The House Committee recommended that Dr. Alexander Hodgkinson be appointed Workhouse Medical Officer (non-resident) and that the Clerk invite Drs. Corker and Riggall to appear before the Board for the resident assistant. Mr. BILLINGE formally moved the appointment of Dr. Hodgkinson as medical officer. Mr. MATHER seconded, and the appointment was unanimously agreed to. Dr. HODGKINSON was called into the room and returned thanks. He said he thought the work would probably be carried out to the Board's satisfaction. If it were not, it would not be his fault. The Board then interviewed the two selected appli- cants for the assistant and resident medical officership Dr. Corker (at present resident surgeon at Rawcliffe Hospital, Chorley, and formerly of Earlestown), and Dr. it. M. Riggall (resident medical officer of Devon County Asylum, and son of the Rev. Marmaduke Riggall. minister in the Warrington Wesleyan circuit from 1877 to 1880). Dr. Corker is 32 years years of age and Dr. Riggall 26. MT. MATHER moved, and Miss BROADBENT seconded the appointment of Dr. Riggall. Mr. DAVIES moved, and Mr. SETON seconded that Dr. Corker be appointed. On a vote being taken Dr. Corker obtained a majority. His appointment was then unanimously agreed to. Dr. CORKER was informed of the Board's decision,the chairman expressing the hope that he would work harmoniously with all concerned and that they would be a happy Dr. CORKER returned thanks and said he hoped to give satisfaction.

Councillor PEMBERTON then proposed the Other resolutions which were carried without opposition. Councillor Pemberton explained that he wished the green for Orford Ward to be laid on the recreation ground off Orford-lane, which was at present in a dis- graceful condition, and it would also serve partly for St. John's and Bewsey Wards. Alderman BENNETT pointed out that the resolution with regard to St. Elphin's was superfluous because the committee had passed a resolution in favour of the laying of a green there. Some members of the Council seemed to think the physical, mental and moral well- being of the community rested entirely on bowling greens and that the way to attain the millenium was to introduce a green in every ward (Laughter.) N'V bile he was not such an enthusiast, he thought anything that introduced glimpses of greenery in the midst of an industrial town and led to healthy recreation was a good thing. Alderman BOLTON thought it was farcical to pass resolutions that the greens be laid for the coming summer, because the necessary formalities could not be concluded in time. The TOWN CLERK said it would probably take three months to get the sanction of the Local Government Board. All the resolutions were passed. PROPOSED EXTENSION OF THE TOWN HALL. At meeting of the Finance and Estate Committee the folloWing proceedings of the sub-committee appointed to consider the question of accommodation for the Health Department were read and approved "The sub-committee made an inspection of Garven House with a view to providing adequate sccommoda- tion for the Health Department." It was resolved— That this committee request the Town Hall, Parks, and Baths Committee to instruct the Borough Surveyor to prepare plans and estimates for an extension at both ends of the Town Hall to accommodate all the depart- ments of the Corporation," and " That the Borough Treasurer report on the probable income from land in Sankey-street when his offices are vacated."

Ald rm-an—BENNETT 13-3,:;;;a the .confirmation of the minutes, and alluding to the proposed extensions of the Town Hall, expressed the hope that the work Would be carried out in harmony with the present architectural features. He should fight against any extension to the very death if it was not to be on the lines he had stated Tho DEPUTY-MAYOR: It is only intended to prepare plans now. Alderman BENNETT also called attention to the reso- lution With reference to the Treasurer reporting on the probable income from the land in Sankey-street, when his offices were vacated, and said that if it meant pulling down the existing premises and allowing property to be built which would have to be acquired by a future generation he should object. Unless they wanted the site for municipal offices, they should keep it as an open space. Councillor PEMBERTON seconded the passing of the minutes.

It had been suggested that the sale of the front land would bring in sufficient revenue to pay for the whole of the extension of the Town Hall. He should object to any scheme of that character. Alderman PIERPOINT alluded to the proposed widen- ing of Market-gate. Architects should be called in to give them designs, and it was equally important that the same thing should be done with regard to the pro- posed extension of the Town Hall. (Hear, hear.) Although he was not prepared to say the Surveyor's staff was not capable of doiog the work it would be rather unfair to call them in, as they had not been trained as architects. Some consideration should be shown to local architects, some of whom were young men and ought to have a chance of making a name by designing an extension on artistic lines. The Surveyor's department was overworked now. Alderman BOLTON said with regard to the proposed extension of the Town Hall the resolution simply meant that the Borough Surveyor would make inquiries as to the requirement of every denartment that was to be accommodated at the Town Hall, and then he would give a general idea of the cost of the extension. Plans would then be open to competition for a proper Council Chamber and the necessary alterations on a scale that would do credit to the Town Hall. They did not want any tinkering or slipshod work. Councillor PENIREREON agreed that the characteristics of the present building would have to be extended in any additions they made. The design was fixed, and the only competition they could have was in the planning of the rooms. Alderman BENNETT said he sympathizsd with the views expressed by Alderman Pierpoint. He did not' think the Borough Surveyor's department should submit architectural designs of such importance ; it was too important a matter to leave to any staff. THE RECENT SUICIDE OF AN OFFICUL. THE DEFICIENCY IN THE ACCOUNTS. Councillor CrIANTLER asked the Chairman of the Finance and Estates Committee when it was going to be explained how the deficiency arose in the Borough Surveyor's Department. No particulars had yet been given except a statement of fact to the amount of deficiency. There must have bee dla considerable lack of supervision. The TOWN CLERK said a report had been submitted and consideration of it was deferred. it would come before the Council in due course. Alderman PTERPGINT, referring to the private agenda, said the minute to be round there was one of the most lamentable that could be placed on the agenda of any Corporation. He thought some explanation might have been given with regard to the circumstances of the death of a young official of the Borough Surveyor's department, and how the large sum of £Bl4 had been arrived at.ln any ordinary,well-managed business concern no servant would have been allowed to take to himself so large a sum, at all events,without having been found out far sooner than was the case titter Mr. Brierley's death.He wished to spare the feelings of his family, but he felt that if ordinary care had been exercised either in the Borough Treasurer's department or in the Borough Surveyor's department, there would have been the saving of a young life—(hear, hear)—and a saving of a large sum of money. He (Alderman Pierpoint) did no not know the circumstances of Mr. Brierley's family but in paying the money to the Corporation, it was a great credit to their hearts, but he did not think it was a great credit to their heads. It seemed to him that

knew that it was called " Market-gate so long ago as 1465 ; that the growth of the town had necessitated a great scheme of improvement, and it was a source of the utmost possible satisfaction to him that the Council were wise enough some years ago, at his suggestion, to definitely mark out on broad and comprehensive lines the general plan and to provide for a spacious central circus. The committee confidently hoped the whole of their local architects would take part in the propoSed competition. Councillor EVANS seconded. Alderman BOLTON wanted to know why they called Market-gate a circus ? Were they going to have a horse track there? (Laughter.) The minutes were approved. THE TYPHOID OUTBREAK. APPLETON WATER QUESTIONED. A WARNING. On the minutes of the Health Committee coming up for consideration, Councillor ROGERS called attention to the fact that there had been an outbreak of typhoid fever in the town, and said there were five patients in the hospital, all of whom attended the ball given by the officers of the South Lancashire Regiment at the Parr Hall a short time ago. He did not say the disease was contracted there, but nevertheless that was a strange coincidence. Since then he believed some alteration had been made in the taps supplying Appleton water to the Hall and samples of the water had been taken. He would like to know if the analysis showed whether anything con- tagious was found in it or not. Whether there was or not the people had been advised through the Medical Officer of Elealth not to use Appleton water for domestic purposes. (Hear, hear.) He knew that Appleton water was supplied to the large works in Warrington and that workmen helped themselves to it. He did not think managers would willingly allow their workmen to drink water that was dangerous to health, and it was high time the Council took the matter in hand to prevent Appleton water being drunk. Alderman EVANS said Appleton water was supplied

solely for manufacturing purposes and their responsi- bility ended at the meter. This had not been before the Water Committee but it had come before the Health Committee, and they recommended that a caution should be placed over each tap. He intended at the next Water Committee meeting to propose that every tap supplying Appleton water be painted red, and people who drank the water would do so at their own risk. Councillor EVANS said the question of the Appleton water was considered as early as possible by the Health Committee, and what Alderman Evans said was quite correct. IVith regard to the examination of the Parr Hall that came out with a clean bill of health. They found no cause whatever that could account for the outbreak of typhoid, and so far as the analysis of the water was concerned they bad yet to receive the bacteriological report. When that came they would lay it before the Council. COUNCIL AND PROPERTY OWNERS.

THE STREET MAKING QUESTION. The Paving and Sewerage Committee recommended the acceptance of Mr. Thomas Stringer's tender for the terming and making of certain streets and passages. It was resolved that in the next application to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow money for private street works the Board be asked to sanction the repayment of the loan within 10 years, and in that event, private owners be allowed 9 years for repayment. Counciilor ROGERS asked if the tender accepted for street-staking was the lowest sent in ? Councillor PEMBERTON said it was not, but very good reasons could be given for the action of the committee. Alderman BENNETT said that with regard to the time for the repayment of loans, he thought seven years was long enough for r.ll practical purposes. He would only agree with the committee's recommendation on con- dition that every builder should be compelled to have the streets made before the houses were occupied. The state in which some streets were left was a scandal. They were like a quagmire, and he thought there was a connection between that state of things and the heavy death rate. Councillor EVANS agreed with this view. There were streets in the town which were in such a shocking condi- tion that it was not safe for children to cross them, and yet all the houses were occupied. Alderman BOLTON said it was not fair that jerry their builders who for ocar theme to the rent as thewnshou olldbd e sh e aabtalehitioleedt h builders who had to pay for street making and keep the housesin a sanitary condition. The streets ought to be made before the houses were let or the builder should have to pay the Corporation the equivalent of the rent which he received before the street was made. Councillor STOTT said he was surprised at the views which had been expressed ,because he was severely trounced when he proposed a resolution to the effect that no house should be occupied before the street was paved. If by extending the time for repayment they could facilitate street paving, he would support it. Councillor LORD said the builders were charged 4 per cent, for the loan and the Corporation borrowed money at 3i per cent. The Maxon : They have to pay 31 per cent, now. Councillor LORD said he could see no argument whatever against extending the period. The owners paid interest for the money and the Corporation should therefore be willing to grant the concession. Councillor WILKINSON said not one atom of blame could be placed on the shoulders of the builder, because it was for the Corporation to proceed with the street making as soon as the houses were built. Aldezman FORsDAW said the Borough Treasurer was able to borrow money at much less than 3i per cent at times. If the Corporation extended the time for , repayment it would be greatly to the benefit of the property owners. At the present time they suffered considerable hardship. Ten years were allowed in many other towns. Councillor HAWTHORN said the object of the com- mittee was to facilitate strest making. It was stated that there was an objection to streets being made because people could not pay the money in time and it was thought that if the committee could extend the period there would be no excuse and the work would proceed more rapidly. The Town Clerk, however, did not hold out much hope of the Local Government Board grant- ing the application. Alderman Bunirox said the extension would be a great help to the builders and all concerned. The houses in Warrington were rented very low indeed. It will be seen that the result of the week-end foot- ball is that Warrington are relegated to the eighth position. If they had beaten Leeds and Salford—as many expected and everyone hoped— they would now have been fourth in the League with the creditable percentage of 6880. Even yet the Warrington men may be considered in the running for the Champion- ship, but personally I have not much hope of them figuring in the concluding tournament. They do not set about matters like prospective champions, and I am afraid that the matches in Yorkshire are looked Attendance at Evening Schools. I upon more in the light of picnics than serious con- tests. Luckily they have only one more match across Dear Sir,—ln myaddress to the Chamber of Corn- the border, and that takes place to-day at Bradford. merce this year I referred to the failure of the State to If Warrington wish to redeem themselves they must exercise any control over children on leaving the beat the Bradfordians Then come the two battles with Elementary Schools as being one of the chief sources of educational waste in this country, and entered a plea Wigan on successive Saturdays. Much depends on that pending such State Control every employer should , the issue of these games, for the remainder of War- make suitable attendance at evening school a condition I rington's fixtures are at home, and none of them of employment. I present much difficulty. A striking comment on this question is afforded by Professor M. E. Sadler's report, on what has been done I in Germany in this direction. From this it would , appear that the chief foundation of the compulsory , system was laid by the Imperial law of industry of 1891 which required employers of labour to grant to their employees who were under 18 years of age the necessary time for attendance at such continuation classes as I might be prescribed by the Government or by the Bye- law of the Local Education Authority. Since that date matters have been carried much ! further, and at the principal centres of the Textile Trades attendance at continuation schools is now com- pulsory for boys up to from 16 to 18 years of age, according to the locality. At Colmar, Elberfeld, Meerane and Augsburg employees within the age limit of compulsory attendance leave the mills early in order to attend continuation classes between the hours of 5 and 7or 8 p.m., while at Mahlhausen, Plauen, Barmen, and Chemnits the continuation classes are held during work hours for the younger shifts.

Broughton Rangers play Rochdale (a), Merthyr (h), Widnes (a), Ebbw Vale (h), Runcorn (h), Widnes (h), St. Helens (a). The Rangers have therefore a better chance than Salford. Hull K.R. and Keighley are pretty well out of the running, and both will probably be beaten a time or two yet. -- - I need not say much about Warrington's display at Leeds. They were thoroughly, and soundly beaten. The forwards played as if they were participating in a friendly and were fairly rushed off the ball by th 3 more determined Leeds men. In the rear, Warrington I were perhaps more accomplished but could do nothing with few opportunities, and against the remarkable defensive display of Young, the home full I back. On his day there is no better custodian in the lUnion, and in two successive seasons he has played a dazzling game for Warrington's edification. From what I hear, one or two of Warrington's noted for- wards may get the "Irishman's rise " if there is not ' a prompt improvement in scrummage work. The six are not working like they were before Christmas!

The number of lessons a week varies from three to as high as six, and, speaking generally, the system appears to be giving satisfaction both to employers and employed. The point I wish to emphasize is that compulsion is not only legitimate but desirable and even necessary where National interests are at stake ; and in this con- nection it should not be forgotten that there is now only a forty-sixth part of the population of the German Empire where attendance at continuatior schools still remains entirely voluntary and that Germany as a whole may therefore be raid, to use Professor Sadler's own words, to have declared itself decisively in favour of extending the educational care of the cammunity over the individual during the critical years of adolescence.— Yours faithfully.

div.p: THE EXAMINER.
FM:WARY Btb, 1908.
Certainly the Opposition THE GOVERN- can have no right to com- MENT AND plain of any lack of out- EDUCATION. spokermess on the part of

the Minister of Education. In the House of Commons, on Wednesday, Lord ROBBRT CECIL, who is as reactionary as his brother Lord HUGH in regard to educa- tional matters, levelled what he considered to be a strong indictment against Mr. MoKENNA. He asked the House humbly to express its regret that the recent action of the Board of Education had not been in accordance with the traditional principles of education in the country. In his opinion, the present chief of the Education Department has not thought it right to hold the scales evenly between those who are dependent on the administration of the Depart- ment over which be presides. The charge made would have been of an exceedingly grave character if it had been sustained by any argument capable of sustaining it. Until Mr. McKsNNA succeeded to his present position, said Lord ROBERT, there was no ground for saying that the Parlia• mentary chiefs of the Education Department had acted otherwise than fairly between the different classes of schools. The implication was plain. Mr. MCKBNNA "hung high among his less abhorred compeers," had acted unfairly in thi, matter. He was a poacher made into a game- keeper, with this further disadvantage as the head of a Department, that he was under the influence of the blackmail of his former associates. The Cecilian way of stating a case is, of course, designedly brutal. We say nothing of its inaccuracy. That will be discerned readily enough. Truth does not require to be stated in terms so inexcusable.

However, Lord ROBERT CECIL'S hard words were like the strokes of the hammer on the anvil, bring- ing out the resonant ring of the metal. Mr. MoKENNA made the most useful speech that has yet come from the Treasury Bench on the Educa- tion question. The note of it was that he had not been placed in his present position to carry out the policy of his political opponents. The Liberal Govern- ment has been placed in power for the purpose of carrying out a Liberal policy, especially in regard to education. There has been no unfairness to Treasury Colleges and particular classes of schools, no holding of the scales unevenly. The money the Training Colleges want is at their disposal. They can have it whenever they agree to the conditions under which it is offered; but if they do take public money they will have to submit to public control. That is the position from which the Minister for Education cannot be moved by any of the unhesitatingly brutal sarcasms of Lord ROBERT CECIL. It is also the position of the Liberal party, which was returned to power, not to carry out the policy of the reactionaries, but to•establish an educational system which should be fair all round, and which least of all should adapt itself to a system of proselytism. The members of the Opposition remind us of Milton's fallen angels shaking themselves into consciousness after their headlong flight downwards. They have not even yet begun to understand that they were hurled from power because the people hotly disapproved alike of them and of their proceedings, and because they desired legislation in the Interests not of the classes, but of the masses. Still in a state of con fusion as to their actual position, they speak as if they yet had the power to command. But the

members of the Government may be assured that they will continue to command the confidence of the country only so long as they maintain the one and the stalwartness of Mr. imam. and Mr. McKENNA. Mr. BIRRELL'S "I won't," and Mr.McKENNA's "We were placed here to carry out our policy, not yours," state the real case exactly. Hard words like those of Lord ROBERT CECIL do not matter. There is no reality behind them. They are sound and fury, signifying nothing.
Since Mr. A. H.CrosfielCi's Tag MEMBER AD return as Member for

BIS BRIDE. Warrington there has been no event half so pleasing to Warrington Liberals as that of Wednesday evening, when the Member's newly-wedded bride was introduced to an immense gathering in Parr Hall. It had long been felt—perhaps more by Mr. Crosfield's friends than by himself—that there was a certain incompleteness about his personality which could only be attributed to the absence of a "better half." The deficiency has at last been fully remedied, and the lady whom Mr. Crosfield has married is already looked upon as an auxiliary force and a delightful acquisition to local Liberal- ism. If the Member had consulted his constituents before engaging in a venture so transcendent as that of matrimony he could not, even with their assistance, have made a more admirable choice than he did' in espousing the charming young lady who is now Mrs. A. H. Crosfield. This is a high compliment—we might add—for political parties have an excellent opinion of their perspicacity. Mrs. Crosfield is both a "Maid of Athens " and a daughter of Lancashire, —a uniqUe and enviable distinction, to which her accomplishments acd personal charm add unmistakeable lustre. It is almost superfluous to add that the people of Warrington welcome her to their midst with that whole-hearted warmth and affection for which Lancashire folk are noted.
MR. R. PIERPOINT We have not heard of any DONS THE likelihood of a Parlia.

WAD PAINT. mentary vacancy in War- rington for some time to come, but our Tory friends have taken time by the forelock and already adopted their prospective Icandidate in the familiar person of Mr. Robert Pierpoint. This seems to dispose of rumours to the effect that when the next contest came Mr. Pierpoint would not be the Conservative standard- bearer. Perhaps his early selection is with a view to healing any breach in the forces and con- solidating the party. There is no doubt that many Conservatives would like to see a Greenall or a Rylands in the field, for Mr. Pierpoint did not dis- tinguish himself during the fourteen years in which he had the honour of representing Warring- ton. He is a man, apparently, of few settled con- victions and little force of character. True he avows himself a Tariff Reformer and a follower of Mr. Balfour. But like his leader he has never yet said what his Tariff Reform consists of and what it involves. There is no doubt on one point, how- ever—that it spells Protection pure and simple and Protection means dearer food, dearer raw material, trusts and combines, more wealth for the wealthy and more privation for the poor. War- rington pronounced its verdict on Protection in 1906, and we believe the verdict will still be the same when the next trial of strength comes. -- Under the above title we HOMES AND Horns. print an article to-day from the pen of Mr. C. E, Parker than whom no one takes a deeper interest in social questions. " Homes and Houses" is suggestive of a burning topic. It is often said that "An Eng- lishman's house is his castle," and in one sense it may be so, but in reality it is of tenor than not a mere hovel. The housing question ranks with that of unemployment, and indeed the two can hardly be dissociated. Still it is probably a fact that if employment were good and regular, there would yet be a large number of slum-dwellers and an even larger number of people living in the "areas of dull monotony 'S which Mr. Parker condemns as unhealthy and destructive of indivi- duality. He pictures the evil of indiscriminate building and describes the root causes of slum areas very graphically, at the same time pointing out valuable lessons for those who read to learn. But he has no ready remedy for the state of things which is a lasting reproach to the first nation on the globe. If he had, he would be hailed as a Heaven-sent genius and benefactor. Progress can only be sure by being gradual, and Mr. Parker does certainly indicate the lines along which the effort of all social reformers should be expended if they wish to see the homes and housesl of English workers a credit to national thoroughness and to twentieth century civiliza- tion. He instauces the town-planning which has done so much in continental countries towards improving the public health and raising the physical standard of the people. Our local', authorities ought to concern themselves as much with the type and style of houses and streets as they do with building lines,which are no unmixed blessing. In the suburbs there is room for both light and enlightenment. Space' air, and sunlight should be all considered and finally every effort should be made to secure for child- life its rightful Eden away from the crowded streets and congested buildings. Mr. Parker has written an informative and suggestive article which we commend to the careful consideration of our readers.

Looking back over the CousaLLOR history of the last half- PEMBERTox's dozen years its seems a VINDICATION. remarkable thing to-day to find the Town Council according a complimentary resolution to Coun- cillor Pemberton, on the conclusion of the arbitration in reference to the Lawson Contract. For a considerable portion of the period mentioned Councillor Pemberton worried the Counciloneeting after meeting, about the waste of money which was going on under this contract and the lack of information to justify the payments. At one meeting he told the Council plainly that,though the contract was for £24,000 and extras, Mr. Lawson's claim would amount to £50,000. He was given the lie direct, but subsequent events have proved that the assertion was anything but an exaggera- tion. A good deal of feeling was aroused between Councillor Pemberton and certain members of the Watch Committee by the former's scepticism as to their knowledge of the work they were supposed to be superintending, and his persistent demand to see the contract, specifications, bills, etc. He even succeeded in carrying a resolution in full Council that all the papers relating to the contract should be open to him, but he never obtained a sight of the essential documents till long after the work was completed. Eventually Councillor Pemberton succeeded in getting an Investigation Committee formed, and as a direct result the contractor's claim for £71,090 was disputed, with the gratifying result recently chronicled. We say without hesitation that but for Councillor Pernberton's determination to drag the contract into the light of day, the Corporation would have been much more seriously involved and might have paid a considerable proportion of the contractor's claim. Alderman Forshaw's proposition—which was carried by 19 votes to 5 on Tuesday—was merely to present Councillor Pemberton with a copy of the whole of the proceedings with reference to the contract, inquiry, and arbitration. It did not seem much cf a testimonial, though it would doubtless afford peculiar gratification to Councillor Pemberton to receive, as a voluntary gift, the papers for which he once fought so strenuously. It would have been a graceful act to have passed the resolution unanimously, for no one can question the bonaftdes of Councillor Pemberton's agitation, or doubt the labour and sacrifice which it demanded, but there was some captious' opposition at the last minute from Coun- cillor Steel—a member who has only been in the Council five minutes,so to speak—and has no first hand knowledge whatever of the course of events connected with the Lawson contract. Alderman Pierpoint made a stirring speech for the motion, , and when the resolution came to the vote, ; Councillor Pemberton's vindication was complete.

Local Clergyman's Bereavement.

Great sympathy is felt with the Rev. E. E. Peters, curate of St. Paul's. Warrington, who suffered a heavy bereavement on Thursday, by the death of his father, the Rev. George Peters, Vicar of the new mission district of St. Thomas's, Wavertree, Liverpool. The rev, gentleman had attended at the Liverpool Town Hall a few days ago, when another of his sons, a member of the medical staff of the Royal Southern Hospital, received a presentation medal for an heroic rescue from drowning. Mr. Peters then looked in the best of health, and his sudden demise will be a shock to a wide circle of friends.

The remains of ex-Sergeant Stuart were laid to rest at the Warrington Cemetery on Thursday. The deceased, who died on Monday morning, belonged to the 49th Herefordshire Foot Regiment and possessed medals for long service, for the Crimean War and the Turkish War together with a clasp for Sebastapol Deceased was 75 years of age having served twenty- one years in the army. The funeral was attended by the Band and an attachment from Orford Barracks and three volleys were fired over the grave. His death has created general regret throughout the neighbour- hood where he had a larga circle of friends.

Junior Liberal Association. ! A meeting of this Association was held at Gregory's Cafe on Monday evening, Councillor Hawthorn pre- siding. Mr. A. H. Rathbone read an article by Dr. J Beattie Crozier from the " Fortnightly Review" entitled "A challenge to Socialism." The writer dealt specially with Karl Marx's " Economic justice " and his argument that the workingman was responsible for all the surplus of labour. Dr. Crozier's contention was that improved machinery with the help of the workingman was mainly responsible for the surplus and that on the principle of economic justice the surplus should go to the •scientists, discoverers and inventors, chiefly, and afterwards to the organisers, capitalists. financiers and then to the workingmen. An interesting discussion followed in which the Chairman, Messrs. H. W. Guest, R. G. Pierpoint, and J. Darbyahire took part. LINSEED COMPOUND' for Coughs, Colds, and Bronchial troubles. 9id. & I/li.
