Handling the subject in an able way he traced the development of English song from the year 1500 and emphasised the fact that we ought to be proud to possess such a wealth of gems of melody. Cemetery Hotel Bowling', Club. Complete success attended the annual ball in con- nection with this flourishing organization which was held at the Lion Hotel on Thursday evening. The atteadance numbered about 150 and dancing was kept pp with zest to music supplied by Mr. A. Starkefs band. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., Mrs. Crosfield, Miss Crosfield, and the Mayor and Mayores were amongst the visitors. The duties of MO's were discharged by Messrs. R. W. Collin, A. J. Jones, H. Wilcox and J. The Pan-Anglican Congress is a great , ten . day's meeting in London of Churchmen from every part of the world. There will be services in Westminster Abbey on June 15th, discussions and idebates every morning and afternoon for a week • 1 and a mass meeting each evening in the Albert Half. IFive of these will be open to all Churchpeople, besides one specially for men, one for women, and one for children. And on the last day, June 24th (S. John Baptist's Day), Holy Communion and a great thanks- giving service in S. Paul's Cathedral. div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

A good word was deservedly said at the Council meeting on Tuesday for two of the junior officials of the Corporation, viz. : the Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. Holloway) and the Deputy Water Engineer (Hr. J. Gray). Both these young men distinguished them- selves in the preparation of the case for the Corpora- tion it the recent Lawson Contract arbitration. In fact the case was so well got up that the Corporation was able to furnish the other side with charts and infolmation, and still wi*n ! *

The Town Hall is not to-be extended suddenly, like the inflating of a balloon. It seems that the Borough Surveyor's department is only required to indicate what accommodation will be necessary to house the various corporate departments under the one roof. Then the architects will be called in to advise as to how the building shall be expanded without destroying its distinctive character as a build- ing. It will be some time before all the departments are centralised and we shall have a big Town Hall when the scheme is completed.

Some funny things are heard at the Licensing Sessions There was a typical sample at the Warrington Police Court yesterday, when the redundancy of off-licences in certain districts was being considered. A witness spoke in emphatic terms of the boon and blessing which one of the houses objected to had proved to the residents of the district, including himself. "If the licence were refused, wouldn't you be able to get any beer ? " asked the Chief Constable. "Yes, but I would have to travel farther" was the reply. " How far?" "About twenty yards." (Laughter.) "Would you go a quarter of a mile ?"—" No.' "You would rather go without?"—" Yes." Strange, but we suppose it must be true. * * * There is much heart-burning and dissatisfaction amongst Knatsford Division Liberals at the recent appointment of Cheshire County Magistrates. When the new list was published recently it was found that out of seven new J.P.'s in the Division only one was a Liberal—Mr. H. Roberts—the others being Messrs. A. Darbyshire (Disley), C. T. Whitley, L. Greening, G. Dakin, F. W. Monks and J. Hepherd. The Lord Chancellor of this Liberal Government has given anything but satisfaction with his magisterial appointments and apparent unwillingness to do any- thing to lessen the disparity in numbers between Tory and Liberal J.P.'s There are plenty of good Liberals of position in Knutsford Division but they have been left out in the cold in a fashion which-. has caused mach mortification. * * * _ _

It is high time that information was forthcoming as to the circumstances which made it possible for the late Mr. H. P. Brierley to misappropriate 74 us. 9d. of Corporation funds, full report is promised for the next Council meeting. Meanwhile the relatives of the deceased have paid back ,EBl4—the sum agreed in settlement of the losses sustained by the Corporation, and the greatest credit is due to them for the honourable course they have voluntarily taken. Alderman Pierpoint pressed for the result of the investigations which have been made, and urged that the blame should be placed on the right shoulders for the mismanagement which had obviously been taking place. It seems to us that with a proper check on the operations which Mr.Brierley superintended, he would never have got into the awful position he did and the fatal sequel might thus have been avoided. We hope there will be a clean breast made of the whole sad business next month. * * *
What we have been tuake-s us what we are.--George Eliot.

Flirtation is the best game for two that has ever been invented —E. Aceituna Grif We have no more right to consume happiness with- out producing it, than to consume wealth without pro- ducing it.—G. B. Shaw. Manners that are noticeable are never good. One should no more attract attention by one's manners than by one's necktie or one's thumb-nails. —Hubert Bland. The secret of success is constancy of purpose. Disraeli.
A man's idea of women depends on the women friends he has had.-3/. Craigie. . .

A man should never be ashamed to own he has been in the wrong, which is but saying in other words that he is wiser to-day then he was yesterday.—Pope. There is nothing more fatal to a political career than brilliant impromptus and spirited oration. A statesman's words, like butcher's meat, should be well weighed —John, Oliver Hobbes. *s* . .

The bargaining by the b-rewers yesterday was in the nature of an auction, but no deal was effected. Messrs. Greenall commenced by a very inadequate offer for the transfer of the Bridge Inn to Gorsey- lane. —suggesting that the Corporation should buy the land at Bridge Foot at market price, and take three off-licences and the buildings of the Bridge Inn in exchange for the new licence. What they prided them- selves on giring was the monopoly value of the Bridge Inn licence and tke compensation for disturbance to which they would be entitled if the Bridge Inn were demolished for public improvements. The magistrates were not enamoured of this ingenious suggestion, and even when the brewers offered to throw the land in— which was something like a real concession —they declined to grant the transfer. What is most evident is that there is an astounding surplus of beerhouses of different kinds round about Bridge Foot, and it would be a public boon if one or two were removed. Mean- while Gorsey-lane district is saved from exploitation by the drink interest. *s* According to Alderman Bennett "some members of the Council seemed to think that the physical mental and moral well-being of the community rested entirely on bowling greens.' It is a pity is doesn't, for the Council has sanctioned the immediate laying-out of four new municipal bowling greens. There is to be another at Latchford, one off Orford-lane, one in St. Elphin's Park, and another on Sankey Bridges recreation ground. All these are due, in a sense, to the pushfulness of Councillor Pemberton who,tired of waiting for others to move, took several wards under his care in addition to the one he represents—Latch- ford. It was a remarkable thing that he should get the resolutions passed so readily, for they will involve an expenditure of something like £2,000. Luckily, the money can be borrowed and the cost spread over a number of years. The greens should eventually pay for themselves, but in any case they will be a boon to theworkingmen of the town and should also tend towards the general improvement of the public health Councillor Pemberton is rapidly making history Electors of Latchford should bear in mind that
will require their votes and interest next November. LINSEED CONIPOUND' for Cough and Colds. Of proven efficacy. Of Chemists.—Advt.

DEBATE ON THE KING'S SPEECH
CON CLUDED. -- The Licensing Bill.

i There was no diminution of interest in the proceed- sngs of the Warrington Parliamentary Debating Tociety at its second meeting on Thursday eveninF. where was a full attendance of members and the public c hen the Speaker (M.r. Charles Plinston) took the hair.

Government considered them to be right and just. (Cheers.) He moved that the question be put. Councillor NIELD seconded. The question was then put as follows :—" That this House presents its humble address of thanks to his Majesty the King for his gracious speech from the Throne," and was carried fleet eon. THE LICENSING BILL.

The Licensing Bill was laid on the table and will be introduced next week. Its chief provisions are :-- (1) Full power of granting, renewing or refusing licences of all kinds including registration of clubs, shall be vested in the local magistrates, the local governing bodies and the ratepayers of the respective districts in the manner set forth herein. (2) On the expiration of seven ye Irs after the pass- ing of this Act the refusal to renew any licence shall not involve compensation on account of that refusal. Licences being granted for one year only, every renewal shall be subject to public convenience as interpreted by the aforesaid authorities. (3) Any licence shall be granted or refused by the magistrates on petition from two-thirds of the rate- payers of the ward or polling district in which the premises in question are situated. (1) All clubs shall be under direct magisterial con- trol, registration being allowed, refused or withdrawn as may in their opinion best meet public order and convenience. (5) Grocers' and other off-licences shall be under the VATIIO law respecting granting, renewal or refusal as set forth in Clauses 1 and 3. (6) No child under 14 years of age shall be permitted in the public or besiness portion of any on-licensed house. The licencees and the parents or guardians for the time being of such children shall be liable to prosecution on proof of a breach of this clause. (7) The hours of sale on Sundays shall be from 12.30 to 1.30 and from 7 to 10 p.m. Total Sunday closing will be observed in any town or district on petition of two-thirds of the ratepayers of such district (8) An appeal against a decision of the magistrates may be made on petition of one-third of the ratepayers of the ward or palling district in which the premises in question are situated. Such appeal shall be heard before a committee composed of equal numbers elected by the magistrates of the local governing body with the head of such governing body as Chairman. The decision of this committee shall be final.

reference to the Royal Oak rebuilding, and offering in exchange for the removal of the Bridge Inn, to give up three off-licences. It was not on the whole, he esil advantageous to the brewer to rebuild a house, the benefit being one to the community. Mr. John Fairclough : Are we to select the three off-licences or do you propose to give up any special ones? Mr. Swift said the firm proposed to surrender the licences of ,William Upton, 14, Knutsford-road ; Arthur Hughes, 63, Priestley-street ; and Melbourne. Brick- street. Two of the licences were, of course, objected to but what he was offering was no light matter. The houses were valuable properties, one being bought • within the last two years for over £2,000. Mr. Fairclough : In case the bench desired would you object to them choosing any other licence? Mr. Swift : I cannot give the Bench carte blanche to walk through the town and pick licences wherever they think it expedient, but any suggestion would be ' seriously considered. Mr. Maginn : You offer three off-licences if you are at liberty to transfer the Bridge Inn to Gorsey-lane. You put it to us that you are acting as friend to the town by doing so. You don't mind my criticising your , offer, do you? Mr. Swift : Not a bit, but I think it would perhaps be better if the magistrates were to criticise my offer in private. (Hear. hear.) I am willing to give any assistance I can. Mr. Magian : The Corporation and the ratepayers will know the value of your offer, as far as I am con- cerned.

Mr. Swift : I have not the least objection to a magistrate telling the public what he thinks as to the value of my offer' but after all, this is a court of law. Mr. Maginn : With regard to Upton's off-licenced house, is it Greenall's property ? Mr. Swift : I cannot tell you that. It is Greenall's licence and if they give up a licence which they should not do they will have to pay damages to somebody. I can assure you I am empowered to give up the licence. The Mayor was putting a question when Mr. Maginn interposed with the remark: Mr. Mayor will you pardon me, and I will ask Mr. Swift to answer my question to me and not to the Bench. (To Mr. Swift): You are mixing this up altogether. Mr. Swift : lam sorry if any member of the Bench thinks I am trying to mix it up. Mr. Magian : We have discussed this before. You are offering the bricks and material of the Bridge Inn. What is the use of a building like that? You want to be paid for this land. Mr. Swift: Mr. Maginn must appreciate the fact that when land is compulsorily taken, compensation has to be paid for the buildings as well as for the land, and this will have to le taken not as vacant land but as a going public-house and the Corporation will have to pay for it as such. Mr. Maginn: When they want it. The Mayor: One of the magistrates wants to know if you will give up the land and the buildings to the Corporation ? Mr. Maginn : He said distinctly no. Mr. Swift : We cannot give the land. Mr. Maginn : The bricks are not worth anything. Mr. Swift : Please don't let it be thought I am suggesting that the bricks and mortar are of any pecuniary value. What I am suggesting is that the entity is of great pecuniary value. If you treat it.as vacant land you rob it of a value which must be in the region of £4,000 or £5,000. The Mayor : Have you flnished.Nlr. Maginn? Mr. Maginn : No I have not. I understand the Cor- poration has not asked for the house and Messrs. Greenall are proposing to make a present to the Cor- poration in order to transfer the licence to another district. Mr. Swift : I am instructed that the Corporation, while not making any offer which binds them, have given us to understand they would like it to be con- sidered.

Mr. Meg= : There are 13 licences within 400 yards of that house and there are no houses between them but Greenall's. You want to take one of the thirteen and present it to a district where there is no public-house and still you assume that we are getting the benefit. I want the public to understand that the compensation you offer is three to one in favour of you clients. Mr. Swift : Of course, the public will understand that is your view, but I don't agree with it. (Laughter.) Mr. Seger Owen produced the plans of the new house and some question arose as to the dimensions, it being stated that the drinking area of the Bridge Inn was 97 square yards while at the new house it would be 129 square yards. Mr. Swift said it was far from the desire of the firm to build a big house and if the bench would like them to prepare plans on lines which would not exceed the accommodation of the Bridge Inn, they would do so. No opposition was offered to the application, but Mr. Swift said he could have called many people to testify to the necessity for a licence in that district.

div.head: LICENSING SESSIONS. BRIDGE INN TRANSFER REFUSED. Off-Licences Objected To.
div.p: LICENSING SESSIONS. BRIDGE INN TRANSFER REFUSED. Off-Licences Objected To.

Great interest was taken in the annual licensing sessions for Warrington which were held at the Borough Police Court, yesterday, and the Court was crowded. The Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) presided and the Other magistrates were :—Aldermen Tinnion, Bolton. and Bennett, Councillors Wilkinson, Evans, Looker, D. Fox, Messrs. H. Roberts, .I. \V. Hayward, S. Wright, J. Maginn, J. White, G. Pilling, E. J. Guest, W. Roberts, C. Jackson Holmes, W. Richardson, J. Geddes, H. Thornton, R. T. Fairclough and W. Furness. The Licensing Committee consisted of the following :—The Mayor, Alderman Tinnion, Councillor Wilkinson, Dr. Fox, Messrs. John Fairclough, J. Maginn, J. W. Hayward, H. Roberts, S. Wright, W. Richardson and C. J. Holmes.

CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT. BEER ON CREDIT. The Chief Constable (Mr. Martin Nicholls) in his annual report (which we will publish more fully next week), brought before them 'a highly undesirable practice existing in the granting of credit to workmen." It would appear, he said, that a licensee had an account with an individual who had his name inscribed in a book, and the custom was for the individual to hand the book to his fellow workmen requiring beer, to take it to the licensee who supplied the beer and received payment at the end of the week at the rate of 24d per pint, whilst the unfortunate workman had to pay 3d. when settling his account with the middleman. The owner of the book made a very considerable income.

Three hundred and thirty persons were proceeded against for drunkenness during the year, a decrease of three. During the past five years there had been a marked increase in the prosecution of females, the figures rising from 7G in 1903, to 110 in 1907.

A SINGULAR CASE. Mr. Browne said he applied under rather strange circumstances for temporary authority to be granted to Samuel Jenks to sell at an off-licence 63, Folly-lane. Mr. Bradburn who had held the licence for many years died last Friday and his widow died on Tuesday. Mr. Steel opposed the application on behalf of Mr. Bradburn's executors and contended that some member of the family should be allowed to carry on the business until arrangements were made. The Bench decided to adjourn the renewal until the adjourned Licensing Sessions.

The Chief Constable said he would give the name privately and handed up a written statement to the Bench.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

'The fortnightly meeting of this Council was held a Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr, G. Pilling. There were also present Messrs. T. Baxter, J. Spruce, G. Egerton Warburton, J. L. Jones, C. E. Linaker, sen. P. Booth, C. Roylance, J. Bolshaw, E. Britch, J. Stokes, J. Whitlow, J. H. Davies, r. Wright, H. Mavvdsley, T. Guest, C. F. Ball, C. E. Linaser, jun., W. Weir, A. Haining, T. Antwiss, J. Mynekyme, A. Norman, G. F. Ashton (clerk), J. Farrington (nuisance inspector), Dr. Adams (medical officer) and W. Diggle (surveyor). Mr. C. L. Evans, of Norton Estate Office, again drew attention to the pollution of a ditch, which had become very much worse since the building of new houses at Moore near the railway station. He had met the Council's inspector who said he would advise the Council that the ditch be cleaned at the Council's expense. With regard to the effluent the Inspector said he could suggest nothing but he (Mr. Evans) asked the Council to have the nuisance abated and suggested that the simplest cause to adapt was a sewerage scheme for Moore. It was very important that the matter should be referred to. _

The matter was left over to the next meeting. Mr. Joseph Hall, of Catter Hall, near Frodsham wrote complaining of the bad state of a portion of Bradley-lane in Frodsham Lordship owing to defective and insufficient drainage. At one point it was not passable. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr. T. Baxter in the chair. There were also present : Messrs. J. Spruce, G. Egerton Warburton, J. L. Jones. G. Pilling, C. E. Linaker, P. Booth, C. Roylance, J. Bolshsw, E. Bach, J. Stokes, J. Whitlow, J. H. Davies, T. Wright, H. Mawdsley, T. Guest, C. F. Bell, C. E. Linaker, jun., W. Weir, A. Haining, T. Antwis, J. Mynekyme, A. Norman, G. F. Ashton, (clerk), W. R.De Prez (relieving officer), and Boyce (acting master).

THE LATE MASTER. The Chairman said that before commencing the busi- ness of the Board he had rather a painful duty to perform which was to move a vote of condolence to the wife and children of their master (Mr. J. Connect) whom they had lost by death. He had been with them for twenty-one years and during the whole of that time he thought he had been a most exemplary master to the house. (Hear, hear.) Mrs. Cunnah had lost a most devoted husband whilst the children had lost a most devoted father. He moved that the Clerk be instructed to write to the Cunnah family and express the Board's deepest sympathy with theca in their sad bereavement. Mr. J. Spruce seconded, and said no Workhouse could have had a better Mi.ster.
Messrs. C. E. Linaker, W. M. Morris, J. Stokes, and A. Norman all supported the motion in sympathetic terms. The resolution was carried the members standing in silence.
.POOR LAW CONFERENCE. Messrs. J. L. Jones, W. Harrison and the Clerk were appointed delegates to the Central Poor Law Conference.

RATE oF 'MAINTENANCE. The clerk stated that the rate of maintenance of pauper lunatics in the County Asylum for the quarter ending Aarch 31st had been fixed at Bs. 51d. per head per week. THE VACANCIES.

The Clerk also intlnrateXl-Ea-t-,--a" the last meeting they appointed Mr. Boyce, the boys' industrial trainer, to fill the position of acting master during the illness of Mr. Cunnah. The Chairman moved that Mr. Boyce be kept in that position until a new master had been obtained. Mr. Morris seconded the Chairman's motion which was carried. The Clerk stated that through the death of the Master both places of master and matron would become vacant. He suggested that he should be instructed to advertise, and that a committee be appointed to consider the matter. Mr. Spruce moved that Messrs. Wright, Norman, Morris, Bradshaw'', Linaker, Pilling and Jones be appointed the committee. Mr. Roylance seconded and the motion was carried.

The hall was tilled with beautiful samples of artificial flowers, and Miss Martin, who was present in the absence of the Mayoress through indisposition, was presented with a besutiful bouquet.

div.head: LATE MR_HOLLINGSWORTEL
div.p: THE LATE MR_HOLLINGSWORTEL

The funeral of Mr. Samuel A. Hollingsworth, of King's-road, St. Helens, who met with a tragic end on Friday morning last, took place at St. Helens Cemetery on Monday. A large number of prominent representa- tives of. the various Roman Catholic Churches were present at Old Windleslaaw, where the interment took place. The service was conducted by the Rev. W. F. Hearne, Rector of Sacred Heart, assisted by the Rev. B. Hornby. The mourners were Messrs. E. M. and B. Hollingsworth (sons), T. Hollingsworth (brother), of Warrington, N. Massey, E. Massey. C. Hollingsworth, J. Massey, and F. Hollingsworth (nephews). The United Alkali Company were represented by Mr. F. W. Stewart, general manager ; Messrs. Grant Paton, A. Thompson, D. Watson, Dr. Brest, A. Rudge, D. Burdekin, T. E. Booth, J. Lucas, J. T. Trotter, S. J Stuart, H. Telford, and J. W. Kynaston, and the bearer were members of deceased's stall—namely, Messrs. Le.. Holt, J. Woolsey, T. Forster, C. Woodward, J. Tic and S. Kinsey.

div.head: IHE INQUEST.
div.p: IHE INQUEST.

The inquest was held on Monday by Mr.Brighouse.- Mr. Hollingsworth's eldest son said his father had been 6 works manager in the town for many years. For fourteen years he had been works manager for the United Alkali Company at Gerrard's Bridge Chemical Works, and had also had charge of the Globe Works. He was sixty-two years of age, and was always of a most cheerful disposition. He was seen to go away from the Globe Works by Walter Morrison, the night watchman, about four o'clock on Friday morning, and John Thomas Keefe, saltcake man, saw him later in the Gerrard's Bridge Works, when he appeared quite rational, and seemed just as usual. Later Mr. Hollings- worth's body was found, at twenty minutes to seven, floating in the canal at Pocket Nook. Mr. Stewart, general manager, said he was through both works on Wednesday, and found everything in perfect working order. There was nothing at all wrong with deceased or any of his duties, and the directors were extremely sorry for what had happened. The jury returned a verdict of " Found drowned," but the foreman said it was quite easy to understand that a man could be blown into the water at this point, or he might stumble in, because the canal embankment was in such a bad state. They sympathised with the relatives.

The St. Helens Gas Committee, who are responsible for the supply of gas in the township of Haydock, have decided to consider a scheme for laying a subsidiary 6in, main, in order to provide a better supply for the district, where there have been complaints of lack of pressure. MR. J. A! SEDDON AND MR. JOHN BURNS. i Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P., speaking at a Labour demon- stration in Batley on Sunday night, said that last week the Labour party had a field day, and it was a bad day for the Liberal Government. Some of them had hoped against hope that one member of the Government would be true to his past. Unfortunately, it had to be recorded once again that the democracy had been deceived. What did John Burns tell them in his unem- ployed days? lie said, "Here am I ; I have been out of work four months, I have not tasted food for twenty- four hours, I am a skilled artisan ; I don't drink,neither do I smoke." And yet the man who uttered this state- ment a few short years ago could get up in the House of Commons and gibe at the unemployed. The Government Must have seen the handwriting on the wall when their majority went down to 49. NEWTON URBAN COUNCIL. The writer has taken it all along and whilst regretting the inclusion of silly cartoons as being unworthy of passing disguisedly to coin a word --into one's possession in such good literary company—has always enjoyed reading it. Paltry pictures are fortunately kept out of the bound volumes. It is passing strange that they should appear at all. JOHN WORKMAN. MUNICIPAL COAL SUPPLY. The cry of municipal coal has been pervading the air for the last few weeks and intruding into almost every society. The " Voice of Labour "has not even escaped, for one " Demos" has been endeavouring to ventilate the subject inyour issue of January 25th. After wasting some sixteen inches of the "column" in reviewing statements made by Councillors at the Town Hall, this "Demos" concludes in the space of one inch with an appeal " to every inteldgent reader to support the proped agitation,"which he says "will humanise the coudinous of the .workers in the coal trade."

It is my intention to point out the utter fallacy of a municipal coal supply. The Co-operative Stores of this town have lately embarked on a coal supply. The Stores is a democratic institution worked by a com- mittee who are elected by the members, and as such can be fairly compared with the Warrington Corporation. "Demos " states that the (coal) workers would have human conditions, etc. I venture to point out that owing to human (?) conditions in the co-operative coal supply, to o of the workers have left preferring the inhuman conditions ot the private traders and shorter hours.

The members of the Co-operative Stores who have placed orders for coal, iu the majority of cases get the same by waiting a week or more. If it is difficult for the Co-opelative stores to deliver coal when oriered, how Much more difficutt will it be for the Corporation, who will be the only source by which every person in town may purchase coal? The intelligent people of this town would rather pay a trifle more for coal than have to depend upon the caprices of Corporation officials for the quality and delivery of coal. Furthermore, if Demos" or any other agitator of individual interference wants proof of the fallacy of municipal coal let them take a census of all those now employed in the coal trade in Warrington, asking them if they are in favour of the scheme ; the answer they would get would soon settle the questian.—Yours, etc.,

- • LIBERTY. THE LA.BOUR PARTY CONFERENCE. The Annual Conference of the Labour Party has now become a most important feature in the political and industrial world. On the Friday before the Con- ference 300 delegates assembled to consider the ques- tion of unemployment and the Labour Party's Unemployed Bill. . _ _

On 'the-following day a Conference was held on Old Age Pensions, when a resolution was unanimously carried in which it was declared that no pension will be satisfactory unless it is non-discriminatory, non- contributory,and applies to those who have reached the age of 65. The Conference further declared that the revenue for pensions should be obtained, not by indirect taxation, but by direct taxation on large incomes.

A number of delegates were present at the two pre- liminary conferences representing Societies not yet affiliated to the Labour Party. They were present, not only to support the questions under consideration but also to support the Labour members in their fforts on behalf of social reform.

The Women's L 'boar League held their annual onfereace at hull during the saute week. The Con- • erence of the Labour Party decided to admit the League as members of the Party. The League was formed for the purpose of helping the Labour Party, and valuable assistance has been rendered by them during the by-elections in which a Labour candidate ' was contesting. When the Conference met at Belfast last year it was I decided to double the Parliamentary contribution per member affiliated to the Labour Party. There were many prophecies at that time that this would result in a decrease in the memberslaip of the Party. The result has been exactly the opposite, as will be seen by the following figuies showing the growth of the party since its formation:

Number of Total Societies. Membership. 1900-1 1901-2 11102-3 1903-4 1904-5 1905-6 ' 1906-7 1907-8 There were 412 delegates present at the Conference, Irepresenting over one million members. The, agenda j contained no less than 88 resolutions and amend- ments. It was decided to increase the Executive ; Committee from 13 to 15 members, and that no mem- ber of the Management Committee of the General Trades Federation or the Parliamentary Committee of the Trades Union Congress will be eligible to sit on the Labour Party Executive. The Conference rejected a resolution in favour of extending the franchise to women on the same terms as men, but carried, oy a large majority, a resolution granting equal voting rights to all men and women. The attem.,t to force the party to adopt a programme to which all candidates shall pledge themselves was heavily defeated.... It was decided to appoint a party agent for the purpose of keeping the electoral machinery intact. Resolutions dealing with old-age pensions, unem- ployment, and the abolition of the House of Lords were unanimously passed. The visitors present must have been impressed by the tact, judgment, ability and enthusiasm evinced by the delegates. The manner in which the business was dealt with would have done credit to any assembly in the United Kingdom. Only passing reference can be made to the Labour Party Demonstration, the Trades Union Temperance Fellowship gathering, the receptions by the Women's Labour League, and the Hull Trades Council. all of which showed the growth and strength of the Labour and Socialistic movement.

Next week, with the editor's permission, I will deal with the Labout party and its relation to Socialism, a subject which has been given great prominence by the Press, and by the opponents of the Labour party. div.head: LOCAL TEA PARTIES'.
div.p: LOCAL TEA PARTIES'.
ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.

A highly enjoyable function was the annual congre- gational tea party in connection with St. Paul's Church which was held in the Parr Hall on Monday evening. About 350 sat down to tea and afterwards a concert was held, presided over by his Worship the Msyor (Alder- man Smethurst, who was accompanied on the platform by the Vicar (the Rev. W. Bracecamp), the curate (the Rev. E. E. Peters), and the churchwardens, Messrs. J. H. Smethurst and John Rigby. A capital entertainment wrs given, and all the artistes were well received. The Lyric Quartette Party (Misses A. Woodland and L. Fairhurst, Messrs. R. W. -Cook and P. J. George) enhanced their reputation by their artistic rendering of several selections, their humorous con- tributions "Toothache " and A bad cold "proving especially popular. Songs by Miss Violet Brown, Mr. NV. H. Ireland and Mr. P. J. George were admirably interpreted, and a humorous duet " Your future husband " by Mrs. Wils,-1 and Miss Lawless created great merriment, Mr. Gelderd appearing on the stage as the husband. The Misses Mary Hadrett, Violet Brown and Dorothy McNeil sang Don't forget the old folks " very expressively, and the patriotic trio " Hats off to the King by Messrs. Gelderd, Cotterall aed Walker affordad much pleasure. The St. Paul's Male Voice Choir did themselves credit in the part song "Spin, Spin " (sung unaccompanied). Mr. E. Wilkes, the church organist, discharged the duties of accom- panist. The concluding item of the programme was the comedy " Anything for a change " by Messrs. Oros- field's Amateur Dramatic Society. The performers thoroughly entered into the spirit Of the play, and the audience was kept in continuous mirth. The cast was as follows :—Paul Honeyball, Mr. W. Tynan ; Mr. Swopping! on (his friend), Mr. G. B. Dean ; Jeremy Census (registrar of births, deaths, &c.), Mr. J. Morris ; Mrs. Honeyball (wife of Paul), Miss C. Rigby ; Margaret Honeyball (sister of Paul), Miss L. Hewitt ; Eliza (servant to Mrs. Honeyball), Miss A. Rowe. ' A vote of thanks was accorded to the artistes on the proposition of the VICAR. On Tuesday evening the annual dance was held in the same building, and was highly successful, thc music being supplied by Mr. Starkey's well-known band. The M.C.'s were Messrs. A. C. Binks, J. W. Robinson, W. T. Flood, S. Bailey and E. Andrews, while Mr. H. B. Houghton proved himself an ellicient hon. secretary.

div.head: WORKINGMEN'S MISSION, BANK QUAY.
div.p: WORKINGMEN'S MISSION, BANK QUAY.

Success attended the annual congregational gathering in connection with this mission which was held in the schools, Thewlis-street, on Monday evening. About 130 sat down to tea, the following ladies presiding at the tables :—Mesdames J. Hassan, David Hill, J. Taylor' Rigby, Brown and Bowyer, Miss lioagh and Miss Charlotte Taylor. Afterwards an excellent entertain- ment was held under the presidency of Mr. ''. Dale,who has for many years been closely identified with the work of the mission. The SECRETARY (Mr. A. Tilling), in submitting a report on the 37th year's work in connection with the chapel, said a review of the events of 1907 did not reveal any feature of particularly striking interest. As compared with the reports presented for the previous three or four years (during which period took place the building of the new chapel, the introduction of the new organ, the decoration of the chapel, and the introduction of the stained glass memorial window) the present report might appear somewhat meagre. They could however, record that during the year 1907 the work of the chapel was carried steadily forward, and they believed that God's blessing had rested upon the chapel. As heretofore, the pulpit had again been filled by friends of many denominations, and the unsectarian character of the Mission had been maintained. The number of members on the church roll was GO. The individual communion cups, presented by Mr. J. J. Crosfield, were used for the first time on the first Sunday of the year. He would here point out that attendance at the monthly Communion service qualified for church membership. The open-air mission band did good service during the summer months, the Gospel being preached and sung in many of the streets of the neighbourhood. On various occasions during the season their members joined with their Sankey Bridges 'Wesleyan friends in open air gatherings which were very successful. The children's Sunday evening lantern services, commenced last season, had been continued this winter and this method of educating the children was one which the members of the mission could heartily recommend as being effective. The Christian Endeavour Society connected with the mission still held its meetings every Wednesday evening, and although the members were rather few, many inspiring gatherings had been held. The accounts of the Poor fund, of which Mr. T. Dale was the secretary, showed that after expending £lO 55., there was a balance in hand of £2 Is. 2d. The chapel accounts stood as follows :—balance from 1906, £5 14s. 21d. ; income during 1907, £77 9s. 7d. ; expendi- ture, c£B2 18s. 9d. : balance ss. In addition £6 4s. 2d. bad been raised towards the new hymn books which would cost £25 10s. 2d. The book decided upon after a great deal of consideration, was Garrett Horder's " Worship Song " and he thought all those who had I seen the book wonld be prepared to endorse the recom. mendation of the Committee. They felt sure the introduction of the new books would add to the solemnity and effectiveness of the services. Their painstaking and efficient organist, Mr. F. !

r Atkinson, had been training about 20 boys and girls to help the choir while the new tunes were being intro- duced. The effect had been everything that could be desired. Mrs. Crosfield (who, they all regretted, was not able to be with them that night), had during the year shown her deep interest in the chapel by again defraying the cost of such items as electricity, fuel, &.c. The Committee desired to place on record its , appreciation of the valuable assistance rendered by Mrs. Crosfield and the members of the Crosfield family as a whole. The officers for the present year were : President, Mr. N. Hough ; Vice-President, Mr. G. Dale ; Treasurer, Mr. T. Taylor ; Secretary. Mr. A. Tilling ; Organist and Choirmaster, Mr. F. Atkinson ; Assistant Choirmaster, Mr. S. Millington; Committee: Messrs. N. Hough, T. Dale, G. Dale, D. Hill, T. Taylor, F. Atkinson, W. Worrell, H. Edwards, R. Tanner, T. Edwards, R. Jones and A. Tilling. , The CHAIRMAN expressed regret that neither Mrs. Crosfield nor Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., was able to be with them. The mission, he continued, was doing a practical and permanent work in the neighbourhood and it was governed on a broad and democratic basis. The whole of their organizations were in a healthy condi- tion, and it was worthy of note that the women's class, inaugurated three years ago under the leadership of Mrs. Moores, bad a membership of 160. He regretted that the men's class had not reached as high a standard and he wished that young men, instead of devoting so much of their time to pleasurable pursuits, would engage in work which would he of lasting good. The Sunday school, it was very gratifying to note, had over SOO children on its books. (Applause.) ' A splendid musical programme was submitted by the Leidertatel Quartette Party, of Manchester (Miss Palmer, Miss Nellie Gibson, Mr. Stanley Boyes and Mr. Brazendale). Their voices blended beautifully in " Voyagers," " In this hour," and "A regular royal Queen," and Miss Palmer and Mr. Hayes delighted the audience with their solos. Duets by Miss Gibson and Mr. Brazendale proved a popular feature. The humorous element was provided by Master 11. Lawton, whose Scotch songs were admirably given, and kept the audi- ence in great merriment.

Shoe-Throwing in Court.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, l'tfargaret Palmer, who was one of the worst characters in the district, was charged with assaulting Police-constable Muskett on Monday night. It was stated by the officer that he saw the defendant drunk in Bridge-street. She was screaming and shouting, and using disgusting language. He requested her to go home, but she refused and struck him in the face. At the conclusion of his evidence the prisoner, who had been violent in the dock, took off her shoe and threw it at the officer. Her aim was a poor one, the shoe missing the target at which it was projected. The magistrates sent her to gaol for sir months.
The Examiner, Saturday February 8, 1908.

div.head: HOMES AND HOUSES.
div.p: HOMES AND HOUSES.
[By Charles E. Parker.;

The great evangelist, D. L. Moody, never spoke a truer word that when he said " You in Great Britain stand more in need of Homes than you do of Churches." The home was founded before the Church and will outlast it. How strange it is that in England, which used to be famous for its home life, and perhaps is still fatuous amongst the favourably situated, we should find in every town certainly in Warrington, slum houses, and not only slum honses, but a great number which are not generally classed as slums, which suggest that all that gives sweetness, beauty, and security to the term, " omit, Sweet Home " has gone. . . _

When a country or a town loses the influences and surroundings which make the dwelling places not merely houses but homes in the truest sense, that country or town loses its most precious asset, its most powerful force for its healthy preservation. Much, if not all, of the greatness of a nation can be traced to its home life. The home is the unit from which all virile states are formed, it is the only foundation upon which the well-being of any enduring civilization can be built. Healthy, pure home life develops the powers and qualities which the world most needs in its for ward march. It is the cradle of the nation's manhood and womanhood. And yet there are few countries in which so large a part of the people are homeless ; they may not be houseless but , they are homeless.

div.head: SLUM HOUSES.
div.p: SLUM HOUSES.

It is not my purpose to dwell further on the unseen but very real features associated with the word home, 'out will pass on to consider the influence of the material structure of the house round which the more spiritual things gather. I want to point out the influence of the house and its surroundings on the home life of the people. First let me refer to those houses commonly known as slums. We do not need to go far to find typical examples of these. I could take you to many houses which are a standing reproach to the people of Warrington, and more especially to those who own them, amongst whom we may number wealthy and respectable citizens. It is not my intention to indulge in an attack on the owners of slum property, although I consider their moral responsibility is great, and I fear too often ignored. The existing conditions are largely the result of bad laws and conditions which have come down to us through the stream of centuries. In the cases of landlords I should think that few of them are earning more than five per cent, net on the capital they have at stake. Old property of this character is bound to have changed hands more than once by death or sale ' • it is probable that many of the present owners have bought, or received by bequest, these I properties upon a valuation based upon the returns in rent, and many are doubtless mortgaged. Looking at the question from this point of view an attack on land- lords would be out of place. Their position is largely the product of circumstances. We doubt not that in many cases the increasing ground value has been transformed into capital value, and has increased the letting value of the houses as ground rents have risen by the aggregation of people in towns. It is possible the present owners have taken these houses at a valua- tion which yields them only a fair return for their investment, but it illustrates our point that through the operation of bad land laws the poor have to pay in their rents a larger proportion of a value ,which has been socially created than any other section of the conomunity. If we estimate the rent as a return upon the cost of the house itself, or rather upon its present value, apart from the land and position, we should find that the return upon this would be from ten to fifteen per cent. Take as an example a slum house, the rent of which is three shillings a week, the present value of the dilapidated structure would not be more than £5O. The rent would yield upon the value of this house 15 per cent, which means that the poor tenant is paying half of the rent for the labour product —the house, and the other half for the position, or as we I call it, ground rent. In regard to the inaction of the Health Committee we can well understand their reluctance to demolish slum property, because they are face to face with the problem that if the poor are driven out of these houses in consequence of their demolition, their only alternative, as they must have a shelter, is to go into higher rented houses. We want to introduce into our congested towns the force of law which will burst the bonds that cabin and confine the people's homes. Mr. T. C. Horsfall makes the following statement : " wing to the influence of slums, our urban popula- tions, which belong to a race which is not naturally more averse to the use of soap and water, or fonder of alcohol than the people of other races, are the filthiest and most drunken of all civilised peoples, and now cantain an alarmingly large proportion of men and women who are unemployable, owing either to physical, mental or moral defects." This is a very strong statement, not very flattering to our national pride. Let us hope it is somewhat exaggerated, but Mr. Horsfall is one who has studied the conditions of the people in many lands, and whether we like it not, further thought and investi• nation will to a large extent confirm Mr. Horsfall's statement. It is a very serious reflection upon the country which claims to be one of the most advanced in the world, a Country in which, we would suppose, the healthy influences of the Christi an Faith would have their greatest influences in elevating the people. If we are, as stated, "The filthiest and most drunken of all the civilised peoples " is it not time that we faced the situation with a view to the removal of the conditions upon which this serious indictment is based? I aim well aware that the question of homes and houses is not the only one, that the condi- tions of poverty, dirt, and drunkenness are by no means solely the result of mean house and miserable environment. It is as true to say that these things make mean homes, as to say that mean homes make these conditions. The truth is that their action is reciprocal, each acting in turn as cause,and effect. I do not wish to exaggerate the outside influences or to pretend that they alone determine the character and habits of the people, but claim that they are very important factors, and you cannot without reservation ' condemn the habits of the people until you have given them fair conditions, given them a chance of develop- ing the good within them. We must cast their experi- ence into a larger mould if we are to expect to develop the healthier life, and an appreciation of social aspirations and civic responsibilities.

div.head: TOWN HOUSES.
div.p: TOWN HOUSES.

I do not want to dwell only on what are known as slum homes, but would rather speak in a practical way of those things which in the ordinary town houses are faulty in many of the essentials which make for individuality, beauty, happiness, health, a larger life for those who live in them. Take the style of houses in which the majority of the working people life. Grouped together, what areas of dull monotony, a total absence of colour, no gardens in which you could even grow a potato. Houses so alike that it is a wonder those who live in them do not mistake their neighbours' fr their own,nothing to individualize the home except a different number. It has been said that " God made the country, man made the City ;" if this be so, would it not have been well if man in making cities had taken as his pattern that God- made country, and borrowed from it all those pleasing features which it is possible to introduce into the towns. What are the characteristics of the country as made by God ? Richness of colour,variety of form, infinite variations in the shape of leaf and tree, plant and flower, hill and dale, and over all the ever chang- ing canopy of cloud and sky. In the main our town houses are built in long , monotonous rows of dingy dwellings with grimy fronts , and grimier back yards saparated by a passage-way from a corresponding long row of similar houses. Such are entirely lacking in that homeliness which characterized the cottages in the country, however humble they may have been, in which the English labourer lived before the people were, by stress of industrial development,congested in towns. In urban districts a great deal has been sacrificed to space, the land monopoly is largely responsible for the monotony and overcrowding of our towns. The houses have been packed together row behind row, often under the shadow of works and big chimneys, which pour volumes of polluting smoke, carrying with it, and dropping as it spreads, showers of smuts and char- coal which the householder has to fight by closing, las far as possible, by night and by day, all possible avenues for the ingress of that air, which if pure, I clean, and fresh would do so much to add to the health and vitality of the inhabitants. This congestion has further resulted in the ignoring of the direction of the streets, of the position in respect to the prevalent , winds, and aspect in regard to sunlight. Sunlight is not so abundant in our English climate that we can afford to turn our backs to it and shut it out by nine- inch dirty brick walls. Sunshine dries and warms, disturbs the stagnant atmosphere by setting up air

div.head: TOWN PLANNING.
div.p: TOWN PLANNING.

And this suggests the important question of Town Planning. The present system, or want of system, of town development is the worst possible. It is an example of individualism being allowed to run wild. Unfortunately our Town Councils have at present no power to control the development of our towns. All they can do is to fix the minimum width of the street, the minimum size of houses and yards, and other details in regard to construction. As a consequence of this our towns are developing in a haphazard manner. The surrounding belts of land are being covered with houses massed together as close as the regulations will admit, with no reservation for open spaces, and no reference to the symmetery of the town as a whole. There is little doubt that some of thel areas which are being built on the outskirts of Warrington will be considered slum areas in fifty years or less. In this matter we are much behind Continental countries. Town Extension Planning is in use in Germany, France, Italy, Belgium, Switzer- land, Holland and the Scandinavian countries. Mr. Horsfall tells us that " Owing to the able way in which the large German towns have been managed by their Municipal Governments, one of whose most valuable instruments has been the Town Extension Plan, their sanitary condition has been very much improved in the last quarter of a century. Their death-rate has been brought below that of the rural districts, and conditions so favourable to the attain- ment and maintenance of physical strength have been created in them,that some of the large towns—amongst them Munich, which has half-a-million inhabitants, and Nuremburg, which has 260,000 —have a larger proportion of young men who are physically fit forl military service than have most of the German small towns, and than many of the German rural districts." Happily by the development of the means of locomo- tion, especially the tram system, the difficulties of , town extension are greatly minimized. The rapid I means of transit has made it possible for working people to live on the outskirts. Town development, , where possible, ought to take the pattern of a star with wide tram routes radiating from the centre with trees on either side. On both sides of the tram routes there should be a belt of dwellings in blocks of not more than six or eight so as to admit free air circula- tion. The house fronts ought not all to be of the Isame size and character forming a continuous line like a street, but be set back to give variety both by posi- tion and style of construction. The intervening angle between the tram routes should be utilized for recreation grounds, gardens, allotments, lakes and woods. By this plan there would be introduced between the dwelling houses a wedge of cultivated land upon which there was an abundance of plant life which would absorb the impurities caused by the dwellings and give bock to the air an abundant supply of life-giving oxygen. We have instances of setting back in our own town, but the house which juts out instead of being treated with a view to its position and made a feature of the street presents generally a blank wall, and if relieved at all,is adorned by an advertisement for Quaker Oats or Fink Pills. EFFECT ON atiLD LIFE

Perhaps the most serious effect of congested town dwellings is in the influence they have on child life. Some figures may be of interest. The heights and weights of several hundred children were taken, those of Bourne- ville, Hr. Cadbury's Garden City, and a slum area in Birmingham. It was found that children of corres- ponding ages measured in height: Hourneville 4ft.9in., Birmingham 4ft. 2in., showing a difference in favour of Bourneville of 7in. While thesame children in weight were, Bourneville 4st. 131b5., Birmingham 3st. nibs., an advantage of 161bs. A further investigation was made in Glasgow and 72,837 children were measured and weighed. This experiment was made to see what effect housing had upon child life, and children from families in one room, two room, three room, and four room houses were taken. In the case of the boys the difference between the one-room and the four-roomed in weight was 12Ibs, the difference in height 5 inches. In the case of the girls the difference in weight was 14Ibs, and the difference in height 5 inches. It would not be fair to assume that these remarkable differences were due to the housing alone ; they are doubtless in part the effect of inferiority of stock and poor feed irg, but there is no doubt at all that the air space and the ' character of the home have a great deal to do with the healthy development of child life, and these things I have been sadly neglected. Happily we ate beginning ,to set more value on the country's best asset. We I are realizing the necessity of giving the children the I best conditions of life if we are to hope I in the future for vigorous men and women.' If those who are older are prepared to take their I 'chance and are content with their conditions, snrely for the sake of the children there ought to be an I effort to surround them with the environment that will give them a fair chance during the period of their physical development. We have shut the children out I of the country, be it ours to open the gate and call them back. Children ought to be bred and reared in close association with nature. The little ones who have no better playground than the streets and no garden in which to see the products of nature's wonderful fertility claim our sympathy. Good work! is being done in the schools but lessons in school about nature are poor substitntc flr actual contact. A boy may take a languid interest in a tree and learn its name from a picture ; he would learn far more if he could climb the tree, be rocked by the wind on the highest bow, and be spanked for tearing his trousers in his climbing. A girl may learn something of flowers and roots from books, and from spscimens brought to echool from the country, but such know- 1 ledge is colourless and uninteresting compared with that which comes from the tending of a rose at a cottage door, or the joy of helping father to dig from the dark earth a fam;ly of monster I ,tatoes. Back to nature and the land is a call to which, as far as daily work is concerned, those who are better employed in forge or factory may give no heed, but the massing of homes in crowded town streets has driven English child life out of its rightful Eden, and back to the land, the garden, the sunshine, and the playfield, should be our motto for the sake of the little ones. I
INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECHABITES.
Warrington District No. 4.

IThe annual meeting of the above district Neel held in the Baptist Schoolroom, Golborne-street, on Saturday last. The Council was called to order shortly after 3 p-n 1 by the C. B. Bro. Joseph Hill, who, in a brief addrs" said that as this was the first meeting in the year 1908, in which he had the opportunity of meeting the officers ; and representatives, he wished every one a happy and ; successful year and hoped that as far as the progress of ' the district and the Order was concerned it would b 3 a record year. On the Roll being called, the representatives from the 20 branches belonging to the district, and also the whole of the district officers, with the exception of one trustee responded to their names. The minutes of the last meeting, also the minutes recording several executive meetings hold during the quarter having been resd and passed, the D.C., Bro. T. Winstanley, presented his report which showed an increase of 51 members during the quarter, also a new adult tent had been opened at Wycliffe Congregational Church. The total number of adult benefit members was 1,375, and the total funds amounted to £5,291 2s. 100. The Auditor's report by Bao. J. Gee, and also the report of the representatives (Bros. W. Wright and T. Massey) to the Provincial Council held in Manchc-Aer were read and accepted.

div.head: BUTT) GE INN L tdENCH.
div.p: THE BUTT) GE INN L tdENCH.

The following resolution Ares proposed, seconded and carried unanimously :—" That this meeting of the Officers and Delegates of the Warrington District No. 4, representing 1,116 juveniles and 1,375 adult member 3, desires to enter its strongest protest against the proposed transfer of the Bridge Inn licence to the district of Gorsey-lane. Considering the number of existing licensed houses adjoining Warrington Bridge, it would be in the highest and best interests of the town and community that the transfer in question should not be granted. The evil would be greatly aggravated owing to the proximity of the Beamont Council schools." The election of officers was then proceeded with and resulted as follows :—Bro. J. Hill, Chief Ruler ; Bro. B. Warburton, D.S.G.T. ; Bro. T. Longshaw, Deputy Rulsr ; Bro. J. Shaw, trustee ; Bro. K. Harrison, P.C. Ruler, Bro. E. Walker, trustee ; Bro. C. S. Fellowes, Levite ; Bro. W. Wright, trustee ' • Bro. J. E. Gee, Guardian; Bro. T. kfassey, treasurer ; Bro. T. Winstanley. secretary; Bro. S. Fernley and A. Ward, auditors.

An invitation given by the representatives of Purity Tent, Brick-street for the next District meeting to be i held n their Tent room was accepted. A splendid tea was provided by Union Tent, and a vote of thanks proposed by Bro. R. FIAR RISON, seconded by B ro. WARBURTON, was accorded to the friends.— Sister Mrs. S. FNRNLEY suitably responded.

div.p: AND OBEDI'

How very quickly the weeks pass; it raw.. seems only a day or two between my weekly chat with my Members. Judging from the past, my Competitions are very popular with you. I suppose all of us are fond of trying to win prizes, no matter if young or old. We have had all kinds of Competitions in the past: prizes for essays, poetry, doll-dressing, drawing, ob- taining new members, etc., etc., but now I want my members to decide themselves the next Competition we have. I am sure all of you have ideas as to what you can do and what you would like to see announced as a Corn- petition. During the next two or three weeks will my members please send me suggestions for a Competition? and to the senders of the suggestions on which I act I will send a very nice fancy box of Fry's chocolate. This is a very easy way of winning a prize. Send me your ideas in a letter or on a poet-card. Any one may help you, but you must remember that the ideas most likely to win a prize are those that can be taken up by all of our mem- bers. Now send me a few lines at once—don't wait I With love, UNCLE NED.

O.RY FOR THE BAIRNS.
"Charlie, Charlie!" clear and sweet as a note struck from a silver bell the voice rippled over the common.

"That's mother," cried one of the boys, and he instantly threw down his bat and picked up his jacket and cap. , "Don't go yet! Have it out!" "Finish this game! Try it again! "'cried the players, in noisy chorus. "I must go this very minute. I told her I'd come whenever she called."
"Make believe you didn't hear," they all ex- " But I did hear."

"She won't know you did." "Let him go," said a bystander; "you earn do anything with him; he's tied to his mother's apron-strings." "That's so," said Charlie, "and it's to what every boy should be tied, and in a hard knot, too."

But I shouldn't be such a baby as to run the minute she called," said one. "I don't call it babyish to keep one's word to his mother," answered the obedient boy, a beautiful light glowing in his blue eyes. "I call that manly; and the boy that does not keep his word to his mother will never keep it to any one else—you see if he does," and he hurried away to his cottage home. Thirty years have passed away since those boys played on the commons. Charlie Gray is now a prosperous business man in a great city, and his mercantile friends say of him that "his word is his bond." We asked hint how he ac- quired such a reputation. "I never broke my word when a boy, no matter hew great the temptation, and the habits formed th have clung to me through life."

RULES FOR GIRLS. Girls, be upright! Girls, be true! Girls, be honest whatever you do! 'Tis better than riches, 'Tis better than rank, 'Tis the best thing of all To be honest and frank. Girls, 'be truthful! Girls, be brave! Girls, be anxious your credit to save!
A liar's a cowar-d, Who dares. not do right;

Be firm in temptatlon. You'll win in fight. Girls, be gentle! Girls, be kind! Sweet in manners and pure in mind. Rough words and bad tempers Keep far out of sight; in play or in earnest Be lovers of right.
-DOROTHY M. GOODALL.
NOT THE ASSISTANCE HE WANTED.

. A traveller passing through a lonely district was set upon by a gang of thieves. -His shouts for help were fortunately heard, and hearing footsteps the thieves decamped, when a man appeared and discovered him tied to a tree.

Oh," cried the victim, "I'm so glad you have come l I've been attacked by ruffians, but when they heard your footsteps they ran away." "Couldn't you get loose, my friend?" "No; they tied me so very fast." "And did they rob you?" _ _
"Only my watch; they had not time to search for my money, which I had placed in My left boot."
"How fortunate!" said the man. "Was the sum considerable?" "Over 12100." "Thank goodness! Are you. sure they are gone?"
"Oh, certain." The man looked round, and seeing the coast clear, said:— "Well, as they are gone, I think I'll finish the job myself "—and forthwith proceeded to do so.
THE SICK DOLL. Of a funny little girl A story I would tell; She was so_ very small, you know,
She couldn't wreach the bell. - Her dolly, it fell sick, And, as is plainly seen, This little mother thought it best
_ To call in Doctor Green. 'The doctor came and shook his head: " Your dolly's very ill; It's leas of sawdust, and," he said., "You'd better keep her still." —JzsSIE GouLBouRNE.

div.head: AND HE DIDN'T DO IT AGAIN.
div.p: AND HE DIDN'T DO IT AGAIN.

A gentleman, while walking with two ladies through one of the principal streets of London, saw a beggar Ipproach. One of the ladies, who had evidently seen the mendicant before, said: "This is the most singular man I ever heard of. No matter how much money ycu give him, he always returns the change, and never keeps more than a penny." " Why, what a fool he must be," remarked the gentleman. "But I'll try him, and put him to a little trouble."

So saying, the gentleman pulled from his pocket a sovereign, which he dropped into the beggar's hat. The mendicant turned the coin over two or three times, examined it closely, and thm, raising his eyes to the countenance of the benevolent man, said:— "Well, I'll not adhere to my usual custom in this ease. I'll keep it all for luck.; but don't do it again." The donor opened his eyes in astonishment and passed on, while the ladies smiled with delight.

WHO TAUGHT THEM? Who taught the bird to build her nest, Of wool, and hay, and moss? Who taught her how to weave it best And lay the twigs across? Who taught the busy bee to fly Amongst the sweetest flowers, And lay her store of honey by _ . .
•, To eat in winter hours? Who taught the. little. ants the way
Their narrow holes to bore. And through the pleasant _summer day
To gather up their store? - 'Twas God who taught them all the way,
And gave their little skill; And teaches children when they pray, To do His holy will.
-ERNEST GOODALL.
WORKED BOTH WAYS.
The Patron was angry, but the proprietor of the restaurant was calm and not the least per- turbed.

" I say," said the patron, "you have some deucedly unmannerly people who come here, or else they're not used to dress suits." "What's the matter now?" tusked the pro- prietor. " I've just been taken for a waiter for the third time this evening, and I don't like it." "Neither do I," returned the proprietor, promptly, "and, furthermore, I won't have it. Why, it will ruin the place." "Of course it will. You can't expect your patrons to stand any such insults as that." " Patronts nothing! The waiters won't stand it."
OFF TO LONDON. Now then, Susie, hold on tight— Off we go to London! Where the shops are big and bright And the: pavements golden. When we get there I will 'buy
Such a 13-ow and arrow; Dolls. for you (or else you'd cry!)
And, perhaps, a barrow. Gee-up, Dobbin, gee-up, ge 1" _ _ .
But Susie cries in sorrow, "Dickie, here comes nurse, She said, 'Wait until to-morrow.'" MAUD PNARSON.

The minister was a great hand-shaker—shut- ting down like a vice. One day he took a boy's hand and gave it an awful squeeze, as he said: "My little fellow, I hope you are pretty well to-day I" With tears in his eyes, the boy answered: "I was till you shook hands with me."
Little Johnny has been naughty, and has to be sent from the table without having any dessert For an hour he has been sitting in the , corner of the room crying. At last he thinks it time to stop.
" Well ! I liope you have done crying now," says his mother. "I haven't," 6ays Johnny, "I'm only resting."

div.head: HE WAS THE VERY MAN.
div.p: HE WAS THE VERY MAN.

A clerical-looking gentleman, in the hope of obtaining a Contribution, entered the office of a newspaper, and, finding the editor in, said:— "I am soliciting aid for a gentleman of refine- ment and intelligence who is in need of a little ready money, but is too proud to make known his sufferings." "Why I" exclaimed the editor, "I'm the only man in town that answers that description. What's the gentleman's name?" "I'm sorry to say I am not at liberty to dis- close it."
"It must be me, parson. Heaven prosper you in your good work," said the editor, wiping away a tear. The parson was speechless, and retired as best he might.
Willy: "I met our new minister on my way to Sunday-school, mamma, and he asked me if I ever played marbles on a Sunday." Mother: "H'm—and what did you say to that?"
Willy: "I said, 'Get thee behind me, Satan,' and walked off and left him."
Pat: "I tell you, the ould friends are always the best, after all, and I can prove it." _ _
Dennis: "How?" Pat: "Where'll you find a new friend that has stood by you as long as the ould ones have?" Laziness grows upon people; it begins in cob. webs, and ends in chains.

div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
NITROGEN-FIXING IN SEA-WATER.

It appears from the researches of W. Benecke, recorded in ~the Report of the Ger- man Botanical Society, that fixation of nitrogen by the action of bacteria may occur in sea-water. It had been denied that such organisms occur in the Bay of Naples, and Benecke has specially investigated these waters. Samples of water obtained from the bottom• at depths of from 65ft. to 325 ft. were added to sterilised nutrient solutions. After three days these were found to contain a large number of the typical nitrogen- bacillus. It would be interesting to know if any of the sea-weeds or animal life of the sea depend for their nitrogen on these bacteria.

div.head: WONDERFUL GAS.
div.p: A WONDERFUL GAS.

Remarkable properties are claimed for a gas discovered by a Lemberg professor, who declares that it is a cure for coniumption. When condensed, the gas assumes the form of tiny greenish-blue balls, which are elastic, like indiarubber, and emit rays, under the influence of which the growth of plants and flowers is greatly accelerated, and organic matter is prevented from decomposing. Some tuberoses on being exposed to the electroid rays in a dark room immediately burst into flower, while specimens of meat whieh had been treated with the rays for two years previously were found to be perfectly fresh, but had lost 70 per cent. of their weight.
CURIOUS EFFECT OF AN EXPLOSIVE.

That explosives sometimes produce curious effects on metals is a well-known fact, but it is seldom that a hole is blown in the centre of a piece of steel. To test the destructive properties of the explosive known as bathe- mite, an ounce of it was placed on a steel plate akoat an inch in thickness, the plate in turn resting upon a cylindrical piece of iron bored through the centre. After the ex- plosion it was found that the hathamite had cut a piece out of the centre of the plate the exact size of the hole beneath, indicating that the force of the explosion had been directly downward. In another test a steel conical shell was filled with the substance and - exploded, the shell being blown into fragments.

div.head: LOOKING FROM THE MOON.
div.p: LOOKING FROM THE MOON.

The mid-day sky to a man on the zn,oon would look very different from the same sky as viewed from this earth. In place of a deep blue vault he would observe, astro-physical experts tell us, a dead black canopy, against which the blazing sun would stand out with a far more dazzling brilliancy and a far greater intensity of heat than has ever been observed on this earth. Furthermore, this black sky about the sun would be studded with myriads of stars, which would shine in broad daylight as clearly as they do at night. The reason the moon's sky differs so much from ours is that the moon has no atm> sphere; at least, such is the generally. ac- cepted theory. If it were not for the atmo- sphere which envelops this globe, our sky would also look black. We would have no twilight, and our shadows would be so dark that even at mid-day we would need lamps in our houses. The sun's light radiates in straight lines witbout bends or curves. But when it strikes (Mr atmosphere it is diffused and scattered &all angles, so that aside from the direct rays of the sun, we have beams reflected to us from all quarters of the sky.

div.head: GLIMPSE OF THE FUTURE.
div.p: A GLIMPSE OF THE FUTURE.

A well-known scientist has been making an Intelligent prophecy as to what sort of a place the world will be in the days oi our great - grandchildren. He has carefully studied the progress of the race from the dawn of history to the present day r---and he has worked out his deductions on the prin- ciple of a proportion sum. They make rather interesting reading, says Cosmos. If we are to believe him, there will be no vehicular traffic in our streets, but moving pavements and a moving roadway, which will carry the people and commerce of the towns. Where one street crosses another, the first will be raised in the form of a bridge; where a num- ber of streets converge, as at Piccadilly-cir- cus, in London, the sight should be worth seeing. Coal will be superseded by electricity derived from natural forces, such as the tide and the sun, and the smoke and dust of• our cities will be gone for ever. Crime will be unknown, for the influences and conditions that cause it will be wholly removed by needed reforms. Trains will travel at four times their present speed, and ships will not cut the waves, but glide along the surface ,- and be propelled wirelessly by electric cur- rents from the shore.

div.head: EIGHTY DEGREES OF FROST.
div.p: EIGHTY DEGREES OF FROST.

It is difficult for the Englishman to form any conception of the degree of cold repre- sented by the 80deg. of, frost _reported from certain parts of Russia. Sir Leopold APClin- tock tells us how, in one of his Arctic expe- ditions, a sailor was foolish enough to do some outdoor work at precisely this tempera- ture. His hands froze ; and when he rushed into the cabin and plunged one of them into a basin of water, so cold was the hand that the water was instantly converted into a block of ice. At —2sdeg., Dr. Kane says, ".the moustache and under-lip form pendu- lous beads of dangling ice. Put out your tongue, and

IT INSTANTLY FREEZES to this icy crusting. Your chin has a trick of freezing to your upper-jaw by the luting aid of your beard; my eyes have often been so glued as to shew that even a wink was un- safe." During a theatrical performance given by the crew of his ship at an inside temperature of —3odeg., "the condensation was so excessive that we could barely see the performers. Their hands steamed. When an excited Thespian took off his coat ;t smoked like a dish of potatoes. Any extra vehemence of delivery was accompanied by volumes of smoke." A CHROMATIC ILLUSION.

M. Gustave Michaud, of the Costa Rica State College, writing to the Scientific American, describes a curious illusion, which he says shows a serious though ever-present defect of the normal eye. With a single stroke of your penknife make a slit nearly lin. long in the middle of a large piece of dark-shaded pauteboard. Over half the length of the slit lay a piece of blue glass, and 'keep it in place with some gummed paper stuck on the edges of the glass, so as to let light pass freely from the slit through the glass. Over the other half of the slit fix in a similar manner a piece of red glass. . • Take another piece of the same pasteboard, and near a corner make two pinholes apart. The apparatus is now complete. Place yourself near a source of light, lamp, or window. Bring the card bearing the two pinholes in contact with one eye, the two holes lying on a horizontal -line, and, through them, look at the vertical blue-and-red slit on the other card, this being placed at a dis- tance of about lft. from the eye and right in the middle of the field of vision. Two lumi- nous red slits and only one blue are perceived. The card bearing the slit may be inverted. The result is the same; the red goes up, the blue goes down, the

lIED SLIT IS DUPLICATED, the blue is not. As everything but the colour is symmetrical, right and left, up and down, on both cards, any observer will promptly reach the conclusion that the cause of the illusion lies, not in the position, size, or shape of the slits or pinholes, but in the dif- ference in colour of the slits.

The inference is right. Owing to its defec- tive achromatism, the eye does not bring red and blue rays to one and the same focus, and the little apparatus shews that this aberra- tion is far from being an insignificant factor of the imperfection of normal sight. If the card bearing the slit is placed at much less than lft. from the eye, two blue 'nits. much closer together than the red ones. 'will DC perceivea. the cara with the slit must be large, to prevent side light from par- tially closing the pupil, thus increasing not- ably the achromatism of the eye.
