• Warrington were fully expected to win at Leeds on Saturday and took a strong team away, but the display given was anything but creditable, and Leeds won comfortably by 11 points to 5 points. Fine weather prevailed, but counter attractions in the City resulted in only about 4,000 people assembling at Headingley. Teams and officials : _ _ _

Leeds—Young, back; Wade, Desborough, Phil. Thomas and Upton, three-quarter backs; Burgess and Wilson, half backs ; Birch, Stead, Webster, Harrison, Brown, and Whittaker, forwards. Warrington--lilley, back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- son, and T ' aylor three-quarter backs ; Brooks and Lloyd half backs ; A. Boardman, P. Boardman, Heath, Belton, Jenkins and Thomas, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Priestley, Salford. Touch judges, Messrs. A. Smith, Halifax, and W. Robinson, Man- ningham. Leeds, having lost the toss, had to play against a strong wind, and with the sun in their eyes to start with, but their forwards soon showed that they were in excellent form. Warrington were the first side to attack. They had chances and were able to make use of them. As a result the Leeds pack rushed to the other end, where Wade made a determined effort to score on the right. He was hauled up a yard short of the line, and a scrummage followed, from which Birch forced his way over, Brown's shot at goal being a failure. Within three minutes Leeds lost their lead. Fish failed at a penalty goal, and a strong rush of the Warrington forwards followed, the result being a try to P. Board- man. The position was near the posts, and Thomas had no difficulty in landing a goal. Warringto n tried hard to increase their lead, but were kept out by excellent tackling. At half-time the Lancastrianaled up a goal and a try to a try. With the wind at their backs Leeds very soon made the running in the second half. As the result of a scrummage near the line Burgess passed out to Webster the latter kicking across. Phil. Thomas raced up, and though he was slow in picking up the ball, he was able ' to register a try, Brown being unable to land a goal. Soon afterwards Wilson got the ball from a scrummage, and opened out a passing movement between Burgess, Phil. Thomas and Upton. The last-named player was knocked over by Tilley, and lost the ball. Phil. Thomas, however, picked up very smartly, and darted over with a clever try, to which Young added the goal. Warrington now played up better, and there was some smart passing between their backs. The Leeds tackling was quite good enoughlor all emergencies. In the closing stages VVilson and Young (Leeds) and Fish (Warrington) were all damaged, Young being the only player who was unable to return to his place in the field. Result : Leeds, 1 goal, 3 tries (11 points), Warrington 1 goal, 1 try (5 points). Warrington v. Salford.—No Score. Warrington played their postponed match with Salford at Wilderspool on Monday afternoon. The weather was wet and stormy, and the ground in a very greasy state. Only about 2,000 spectators assembled to witness a very keenly-contested but pointless game. Both teams were strongly represented, Watring- ton's side being exactly the same as Saturday. Salford's selection was as follows: Mason, back ; Cook, W. Thomas, Lomas, and Hyam, three-quarter backs ; Preston and John, half backs ; E. Thomas, Buckler, Lees, Spencer, Warwick, and Harris, forwards. Referee : Mr. Clegg, Manningham. Warrington had the advantage of a strong breeze during the first half, and Lomas, Mason, and Cook were constantly defending. Eventually some brilliant for- ward play by Spencer, Warwick, and Rees caused Fish to save, whilst Tilley was lucky to check John near the line. Warrington again took up the running, and from a passing movement Fish was forced into touch near the corner flag. Salford continued to defend stubbornly, and after Thomas had failed twice from penalty shots, Tilley dribbled through, but was robbed over the line by Thomas. At half-time there was no I' score. Turning round Salford made strong play at the War- rington end, but like the opposition their play lacked finish. Eventually the home vanguard improved, and Jenkins was pulled up near the posts. Thomas missed another penalty, whilst both Watkin and Fish were checked near the corner. The Salford forwards responded splendidly, and a vigorous rush almost over- came Tilley's defence. Mason failed to field twice in quick succession, and the Salford goal had remarkable escapes. Salford once again renewed the attack, and John almost dodged through. Lomas again tailed with a penalty kick, and the result of a hard gams was a pointless draw.

FRIENDLY MATCH.

WARRINGTON " A " V. HGERTON.—Warrington "A ' were at home to Egerton OD Saturday,and a good crowd assembled in fine weather. During the first half the visitors were hard pressed, and a psssing movement in the first minute led up to a try to Kenyon, Jordan placing a goal from the extreme angle. Warrington continued to prove themselves the superior team, and after Jordan had hit the posts with a drop at goal, Forster, who was deputizingiat centre, scored a good try from near half way. Jordan crossed after clever work by Lloyd, and Forster gosling, the locals led at half-time by two goals three tries (13 points) to nil. Tnrning round the visitors first took advantage of some weak play by the home custodian, and the ball was taken over, the try not being converted. After this the locals pressed, and a couple of fine runs by Lloyd caused the visitors to defend. Lloyd scored after a brilliant effort, and near the close Forster added his second try, and Warrington won by 23 points to three points.

Mrs. PARKER then read the address as follows : Presented to Arthur H. Crosfleld. Esq., M.P., together with a grand piano on the occasion of his marriage. Sir, We the undersigned representing the various Liberal organizations of Warrington would recall the great services which the family you represent have rendered to the Liberal cause in this borough. We remember the gallant fight which in 1900 you made to secure the Parliamentary representation for the party of reform. Although unsuccessful on that occasion, you again in 1906 cheerfully responded to our call. Your energy, your loyalty to Liberal principles so consoli- dated the forces of progress that an enthusiastic and , united party were able to place you at the head of the 1 , poll by a majority of 1,500. (Applause.) Warrington, February sth, 1908." , (Applause). MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH.

THE CHAIRNIAN"S ADDRESS. THE TORIES AND THE PRICE OF BREAD. The CH kinMAN said he had received a very kind letter from Mr. W. Long who offered his hearty con- gratulations to the bride and bridegroom, arid also a letter from Councillor Toole, who, it appeared. was taking the chair at a lecture on Athens. (Laughter). Athens seemed to be very much to the fore at present. (Laughter). They had songs, lectures and meetings about it, they had the beautiful Greek flag above the platform, and, best of all they had got the maid of Athens with them. (Applause). They all recognized that that meeting was of a social rather than a political character. (Hear, hear). They were met to extend a , hearty welcome to Mr. and Mrs. Crosfteld—(applause) —but being a bit of a politician, he (Mr. Parker) could not altogether overlook the fact that it was not only Mr. Arthur Crosfleld whom they were greeting, hut they were welcoming amongst them the member for War- rington—(lond applause)—the man who two years ago stood for Free Trade—(applause)—for free food and for food at its natural price. (Applause). He thought they could congratulate themselves on adhering to that policy on account of the illustrations they had had during the past few years. He specially referred to the rise in the price of bread. The Tory party had, in his ' opinion, made a very unworthy use of that fact. (Hear, hear.) The rise in the price was entirely due to the shortage of the world's crop, caused in most countries by a shortage of sunshine. The deficiency in the crop was about 46 million quarters, and the advantage we had as a country which drew its supplies from the ' whole world and put no barrier on their coming in, was illustrated by the fact that bread during the past year had in England been cheaper than in any importing country in the world. (Applause). In Germany, where the duty was lie. ed. per quarter, the rise had been 3s. inore than in England, and that illustrated the absurdity of making believe that the foreigner would pay the duty. (Applause.) Taking the duty and the extra increase, the price which the Germans paid for their corn and their bread during this scarcity was about 40 per cent. higher than in England. (Applause.) The leaders of the Tory party. knew very well—anybody with an ounce of brains knew very well—(applause)—that the rise in bread had not been the /result of Liberal Government. But while they knew that fact, they bad not hesitated to make nse of the votes which their canvassers and underlings bad procured by trying to make out to ignorant electors that the Government was to blame for the increased price of corn. (A voice: " Shame on them.") He thought it was a shame. (Hear, hear.) The Tories never knew how to play the game. They were always getting on the off-side—(laughter)—and they knew it. Turning to the more personal and agreeable work of the evening, Mr. Parker heartily welcomed the bride and bridegroom. " I have," he continued,. "always found our Member very considerate in asking my advice on any important step that he takes—(laughter)—and I

I Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P., who MS received with I loud cheers and the singing of" For he's a jolly good I fellow," said he honestly felt it was beyond his power to find words to express adequately, on behalf of his wife and himself, their gratitude for the beautiful i presentation which had been made to them, and for the warmth and kindness of the greeting they had received.. He could assure the assembly that they would value the present all their lives, and very greatly, in the first , place because it came to them from such a large number ,of their friends in Warrington, and in the second place 1 because he thought the choice was so happy. As Mrs. I Parker had said, they might have had a beautiful okiet d'art in the way of plAte, which they would have kept carefully under lock and key and had a look at every now and then. (Laughter.) Such a present would have been a pride and a pleasure to them, but in this case their friends had given them something which would be a source of constant pleasure to both of them in London, and particularly to his wife, because she was devoted to music—(applause)—and be dare say some of them knew that music had always been one of his own hobbies in life. (Hear, hear.) The gift was therefore, if he might venture to say so, particularly appropriate and it would be the greatest possible source of enjoy- ment to them day by day when they were trying to represent the people of Warrington as well as they , could in London. (Applause.) May I thank you , now " continued Mr. Crosfleld 4 for the greeting that you have given to my dear young wife. I was wonder- ing whether I ought to introduce her to you as A MAID OF ATHENS

—(laughter). You have heard a great deal about Athens this evening aad perhaps you know that there are ties which link her to that land of song and beauty, whose ancient civilization is still the wonder and the
imperishable glory, as it is the priceless possession of

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, February 8, 1908. MESSRS. CROSFIELDS' "'WEI:ME i NOTES ON GAMES AND WARRINGTON BRIDGE. ENTERTAINED. , , ATHLETICS. i THE MAYOR AND MESSRS. Dinner and Concert Last Night. 1 FAIRCLOUGH. I Nothing to Withdraw.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, February 8, 1908. MESSRS. CROSFIELDS' "'WEI:ME i NOTES ON GAMES AND WARRINGTON BRIDGE. ENTERTAINED. , , ATHLETICS. i THE MAYOR AND MESSRS. Dinner and Concert Last Night. 1 FAIRCLOUGH. I Nothing to Withdraw.

the whole civilized world. (Applause). But I would like to remind you, what has not been mentioned to-night, that on the other hand she was born in old Lancashire—(applause)—and that her earliest years were spent almost within a stone's throw of our own town, so that, listening to your welcome to-night, I could not help feeling that after all, perhaps, she was coming back to her own kith and kin. (Applause). Then, as regards myself, it has been a great relief to be met with such great kindness and heartiness, because friends of mine who have been poking fun at me lately,—as they are apt to do on these occasions—(laughter)—said that as I had been seeking a little protection—(laughter)—from what Shakespeare ought to have called the state of single unblessedness " your faith in my Free Trade principles might be shaken—(laughter)—and further that as at the last election I did stand for reasonable individualism, which I still believe in, there might appear to be something a little inconsistent in the step one has taken. (Laughter). I would, however, venture to remind you that I always stand for qualified individualism—(laughter)—and I hope you will agree with me that we have a practical and pleasing illustration of it this evening. (Applause). Then, if we come to what one hears a great deal of—and rightly so—nowadays and what we all believe in—social reform—it occurs to me that there is no happier illustration of social reform than matri- mony. (Laughter.) Allusion has been made by Mrs. Parker to the comradeship that is offered by the Women's Liberal Association to my wife, and I would like to take the opportunity of telling you frankly that both by training and, if I may so express it, by natural sympathy and inclination, my wife is A THOROUGHLY GOOD LIBERAL.

(Loud Applause.) I know that whether we are here in Warrington or whether we are trying to the best of our abilities to serve you in London, all that concerns the welfare and well-being of our fellow-townsmen will always have her sympathy and deep interest and support, so far as she can give it. (Applause.) Continuing, Mr. Crosfield said the other day he reminded their president that he (Mr. Crosfleld) offered to come and answer for his political sins, if Mr. Pat-1/4er thought it a fitting occasion. Mr. Parker, however, said :—" Certainly not. I am quite sure that if there is a prospect of hearing your wife give us a piece on the piano, you will not be listened to if you treat us to any long disquisition on your work during the last twelve months." (Laughter.) So that was a little treat to be kept in store for a few weeks. He was not, however, going to shirk his duties —(applause)—either this year or at any time, and while one noticed an inclination on the part of their friends the Tories to go about talking as if the Liberals ought to dress themselves in "the candle and winding sheet of repentance "and cry of Peccavi "he for his p irt took an absolutely different view of the case. (Applause.) They had heard a good deal lately about

Last evening marked a red letter occasion in the history of Messrs. Joseph Crosdeld and Sons Ltd., the whole of the employees being entertained at dinner by Mr. A. H. Oros&ld M.P., in celebration of his recent

At the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening, the Mayor alluded to the much vexed question of the widening of Warrington Bridge which had been before the General Purposes Committee. He pointed out that a letter had appeared in the Press from Mr. R. T. Fairclough. He (the Mayor) had nothing to withdraw from what he said before the Chamber of Commerce, and be thought the statement that Mr. Fairclough now made had proved the wise and judicious care that the Bridge Committee was taking. It was quite true that Messrs. Fairclough bad offered £l,OOO, but the Bridge Committee did not think that offer was good enough. (Hear, hear.) Before the Chamber of Commerce the statement was made that if they could widen the bridge to allow barges of 300 tons instead of 100 tens to pass under it, there would be a saving of £7 10s. for every passage-6d. per ton on 300 tons. If they had two barges of 300 tons the saving would be £l5, and that meant Messrs. Fairclongh would , save £7BO a year. Therefore he (the Mayor) thought the Council would see that the committee I acted wisely in not spending from £lB,OOO to £20,000 to benefit these people. (Hear, hear.) If Messrs. Fairclough and those who took barges under the bridge would grant to the Corporation 6d. per ton on cargoes that went under the bridge for seven or ten years he would do his best to ',,et the Bridge Committee to go in for a new bridge. But when they wanted the Council to spend from £lB,OOO to £20,000, according to Mr. Fairclough's statement the Committee were wise in refusing the offer of £l,OOO. Councillor PEMBERTON said he agreed with every word the Mayor had said. As one who pressed the matter forward, he was glad the Council had taken up such a position. If Messrs. Fairclough and adjoining owners were to give £lO.OOO towards the bridge it would cost, at 4 per cent, £4OO per year, and between them they would save £l,OOO a year. The Corporation ought to do everything they possibly could to encourage the manufacturers of the town, but it was not right they should give undue preference to one or two. If the traders found £lO,OOO the Corporation could make a bridge of one span— The MAYOR : Excuse me. I only wanted to make that statement. I don't want any discussion on it. Councillor PEMBERTON : I was going to say some- thing about the position of a certain gentleman in the firm holds, deputed from this Council. The MAYOR : I think we shall do our best.

The matter then dropped. When the minutes of the Rivers Committee came up for confirmation, Alderman BOLTON drew attention to report of Mr. R. T. Fairclough as representative of the Corporation on the Upper Mersey Navigation Com- mission and said Mr. Fair°lough seemed to be a good man for that purpose. Councillor PEMBERTON said he did not agree. He contended that Mr. Fairclough was using his position with Admiral Nares to do everything he could to stop , the bridge and it was a great mistake of the town to appoint him to the position. Alderman BOLTON: He understands the river and it is to his own interest as well as ours to see that the river is properly dredged. The TOWN CLERK : Admiral Nares has nothing to do with the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission. The minutes were approved. The Council unanimously approved the General Pur- poses Committee's decision that formal application be made to the Acting Conservator of the Mersey for his approval of the plans for the widening of the bridge.

div.head: MID-DEVON.
div.p: MID-DEVON.

The Tories were chuckling over the result of that contest and possibly they might chuckle over one or two other by-elections, but personally he believed a good many Canservatives thought the least ssid about :\ lid-Devon the better. (Applause.) He wondered what would be said, if the Liberals on their side indulged in the kind of tactics that had been adopted in Mid-Devon ! He felt that a party must indeed be in very sad straits when they they were so hard put to it that they had to resort to such deliberate mis-statements as were used there. (Applause). Then their opponents said: "Oh, but look at home. What did you say at the last election ! " Well, all he said in Warrington, and every word he said during that election, he stood by. (Loud applause.) There was not one syllable in connection with South Africa, Chinese Labour, Ireland, or any of the topics on which the Tories were trying to get up a little agitation against the Free Trade party—not a single word that he ventured to address to audiences in Warrington during the General Election that he did not absolutely adhere to. (Applause.) He hoped the Liberal party would always stick to tactics of that kind, and he would be thoroughly ashamed to go on a platform in Warring ton and say a word that he did not mean and that he was not prepared to stick to. (Applause.) He would not that evening go into political details, but he would say in passing that the

div.head: ATTEMPT TO ATTACK TrlE_ GOVERNMFNT
div.p: ATTEMPT TO ATTACK TrlE_ GOVERNMFNT

on the question of Chinese labour had absolutely exploded—(applause)—and in their desperate straits the Tories had now made an attempt to villify Mr. Birrell and get up all kinds of prejudice—the old anti-Irish prejudice that had done duty so long in the Tory party. (Hear, hear.) In the House of Commons this week they had had a masterly and magnificent speech from Mr. Birrell exploding the whole thing, and he would commend those utterances to the careful attention of all who could find time to study them. It was also worth everyone's while to read the almost epoch-making speech on the same question by Lord Dudley in the House of Lords. (Applause.) Mr. Parker had alluded to Free Trade, and they knew that with all the issues and all the complex questions that were ahead of them, it was mainly on the great Free Trade issue that they fought the last election. "If they are pleased with an occasional by-election " continued Mr. Crosfleld, " sell, I don't want to say anything unkind on a night like this, even of my political opponents, but I am afraid there will be a

div.head: RUDE AWAKENING
div.p: RUDE AWAKENING

for these political Rip Van Winkles, who think they can resuscitate in England the old, played out system of Protection, when they come to the next election, and when it will by no means be a question of gulling a stray electorate and persuading them that the Liberal party is responsible for the seasons. (Laughter.) Then once more you will have to face the simple issue—shall we increase the price so much for your hoots and shoes and stockings, and dress,and meat and bread; will you do this in order to introduce gradually into this country the system of trusts which has been fastened on the people in America, and the charming system of palm oil and bribery and corruption which vitiates the whole legis- lature at Washington ; will you make everything dearer for the poorest people in order to introduce these systems? The answer will be the same as it was on the last occasion and nowhere, I venture to sax, will that answer be more emphatic than in the 'County, Palatine of Lancashire. (Loud applause.) There is no- one in the House of Commons who appreciates that situation more thoroughly than the extremely astute, the extremely able and wonderfully clever leader of the Opposition himself. The game he has played in the Flouse of Commons during the last few years has been extraordinarily clever,but I think at times he must also I regret that he did not take the simple line at the start and say 'I see through it and it won't do.' (Applause.) I do not want to suggest because one speaks so often of Free Trade that any of us Progressive Liberals are shirking the

div.head: OTHER PROBLEMS.
div.p: OTHER PROBLEMS.

We look them fairlY;;;lT-s41.;;;Ii-itc the face, and I am sure you have on the Liberal side in the House of Commons a great band of men who will bring to the study of these questions knowledge and genuine sym- pathy as well as prudence and commonsense without which they cannot be honestly and fairly dealt with. (Hear, hear.) It will be a great pleasure to accept the invitatioh that has been given to me this evening to come down in a few weeks time to discuss some of these great questions of the day, so full of interest, so vital in their importance to the whole nation. Broadly speaking, I feel that the Liberal party,which is in better fig and more full of work to-day than it ever was in its history, without deviating into the arid and sterile region of Non-possumus and selfish reaction on the one hand, or on the other losing itself in misty swamp and treacherous, quaking bog, and unfathomed quagmire of revolution, will steadily go forward through fertile and promising country to the good and useful work that lies before us. (Loud applause.) Once more I wish to thank you on my own account but still more on behalf i of my dear young wife, for the exceeding great kindness i and cordiality with which you have received us this I evening. It is indeed a red letter day for both of us, land we thank you from the bottom of our hearts." (Loud Applause.)

div.head: MRS. CROSFIELD AS PIANIST.
div.p: MRS. CROSFIELD AS PIANIST.

Mrs. Crosfield then in response to the cordially expressed wish of the audience gave a pianoforte solo in a way which demonstrated that she is a true artiste and a brilliant executant. Then the cry of " Encore " was so persistent that she obliged with another selection which afforded equal pleasure. THANKING THE ARTISTES.

Councillor EVANS proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman and artistes and also joined in the general congratulations to Mr. and Mrs. Crosfleld. Mr. JOSEPH HOWES seconded and said that in taking this step Mr. Crosfleld had obeyed the mandate of the constituency. (Laughter.) Referring to the activity of the Tories, he said he welcomed activity in the political world. As Liberals they had a case so strong that they could defend it at any point at any time and it could not be successfully impeached by argument. (Applause.) The vote was carried with great enthusiasm and the meeting closed with the Natiotal Anthem.

div.head: PRESENTAIION PIANO.
div.p: THE PRESENTAIION PIANO.
The Steinway grand piano which has been presented to Mr. and Mrs. Crosfleld has been purchased through Mr. R. H. Pearson, Bridge-street, Warrington. KING'S CHIMNEY ON FIRE.

One of the Ring's chimneys was on fire at Windsor Castle on Thursday morning. The ni&ht watchman was alarmed by the quantity of smoke which poured out of a kitchen chimney, and when the castle and town brigades got to work they found a large oak beam in the huge chimney was smouldering beneath the State apattments on the north side of the Castle. The fire was soon extingrished.

div.head: DEATH OF DR. BRAIDE.
div.p: DEATH OF DR. BRAIDE.

A. painful sensation was created on Tuesday even- ing by the death after a very short illness of Dr. George Braide who passed away at his residence, Bold-street, at five o'clock. To the doctor's many friends the news came as a great shock,for few were aware of his serious illness. Last week he was attending to his professional duties as usual and appeared to be in good health and cheerful spirits. On Saturday he took to his bed owing to an attack of influenza, and pneumonia supervened. He was attended by Dr. Bowden, and on Tuesday Drs. Langdale and Peacocks were called in, but their united efforts were unavail- ing, and Dr. Braide passed away at the time stated. The doctor, who was 42 years of age, was a son of Mr. Edward Braids, formerly goods manager for the Warrington District of the London and North-Western Railway Company. He was educated at the Grammar School and afterwards at Owen's College, Manchester, where be qualified as a medical man, and he com- menced private practice in Warrington about eighteen years ago. For a considerable time be discharged the duties of medical officer at the Union Workhouse, but he resigned the position about eighteen months ago when the Guardians decided to appoint a resident medical officer. He, however, retained the office of medical officer to the No. 2 District of the Union. He was a prominent Freemason, and at the time of his death was senior warden of the " Gilbert Greenall " Lodge 1250. He was a staunch Conservative and a Churchman. His unassuming, genial and sympathetic disposition gained for him the highest esteem of all with whom he came into contact, and many have lost in him a true friend. With his widow, who is a sista of the late Mr. Arthur Shawcross, Sankey-street, as well as with his parents and only surviving brother, the deepest sympathy is felt in their great bereave- ment.

div.head: GUARDIANS' CONDOLENCE.
div.p: GUARDIANS' CONDOLENCE.

At the meeting of the Board of Guardians on Wednesday, Mr. J. Billinge intimated the melancholy news of ,the late resident medical officer and the medical officer for No. 2 district, Dr. Braid°. He thought he was expressing the sentiments of his colleagues when he said how deeply sorry they were. His association with Dr. Braide went back twelve years. In both pleasant and painful circumstances he had entered into communication with him and he had always found him courteous and obliging. They deeply mourned his loss and in offering their sincere sympathy to Mrs. Braide and the relatives, they trusted that the great Head of the Church in this very trying dispensation might afford to them the help they stood in need of at this moment. He moved that a vote of condolence be forwarded to the widow.

Nfr. MATitErt seconded and said every member and official felt the loss which had fallen upon them and deeply sympathised with the widow and parents. The vote was carried in silence, all the members standing.

REFERENCE AT THE BLUE COAT SCHOOL. Mr. Charles White, who presided over the annual concert in connection with the Blue Coat School on Wednesday eveuina, referred in sympathic terms to the death of Dr. Braide who had been the medical officer of the school for a long period. He always took great care of the scholars and he was sure they would miss him very much indeed as he was a very I kind roan.

div.head: THE, FUNERAL.
div.p: THE, FUNERAL.

The funeral of the deceased doctor took place at the Warrington Cemetery at 1 p.m. yesterday amid extraordinary manifestations of sympathy and regret. There was a very large gathering of mourners and friends at the graveside where the last rites were conducted by the Rev, W. Bracecamp. The chief mourners were C. Braide (father), :arr. J. Braide (brother), Mr. Cr. Braicle, Garston, (cousin), Mr. Harvey Braide (cousin), Mr. R. Stott (Manchester), and 111,-.. J. Carter.

A number of public bodies with which the deceased gentleman was officially connected were strongly represented at the graveside, including the Medico- Ethical Association, the local lodge of Free Masons' the London and N orth-Western Railway Company, the Board of Guardians, and Rural District Counc ii An immense number of wreaths were sent as a last tribute of respect. The coffin, which was of fumed oak with brass mountings, was supplied by Mr- H. F. Greenoug,h.

div.head: Hand of Hope Union.
div.p: Hand of Hope Union.

The quarterly Council meeting of the Warrington Band of Hope Union was held in Gregory's Café on Thursday under the presidency of the Rev.J.S. Hughes, the President (Mrs. James Dodds) being absent through indisposition. A vote of sympathy was forwarded to the Secretary (Mr. Gandy), his wife being ill.—Mr. Hamlet produced a report of the meeting of the United Kingdom Band of Hope Union, to which he was a delegate.—The Assistant Secretary (Mr. Wooley) intimated that the arrangements for the festival to be held in the Parr Hall in May were well in hand, and said he thought it would be the best they had ever had. A resolution was passed appealing to the Licensing Bench to reduce the number of off-licences in the town. - A vote of thanks to Mr. Hamlet for his report concluded the meeting.
For Chronic Chest Complaint, Woods' Great Peppermint Cure.—Advt.

I need not say much about Warrington's display at Leeds. They were thoroughly and soundly beaten. The forwards played as if they were participating in a friendly and were fairly rushed off the ball by the more determined Leeds men. In the rear, Warrington were perhaps more accomplished but could do n )thing with few opportunities, and against the remarkable defensive display of Young, the home full back. On his day there is no better custodian in the Union, and in two successive seasons he has played a dazzling game for Warrington's edification. From what I hear, one or two of Warrington's noted for- wards may get the "Irishman's rise " if there is not a prompt improvement in scrummage work. The six are not working like they were before Christmas!

Burgess was the most pleased man on the field at Leeds and did not play a bad game in his rough and ready style. flow is it, I wonder, that a man takes special joy in bringing about the downfall of his old club-mates? Watkin has his first trial with the premier team and gave a satisfactory display, though few opportunities came his way.

Monday was such a shocking day for football that the important match with Salford was spoiled from the spectators' point of view. Both teams were repre- sented exactly as on Saturday, and proved very evenly matched in the mud and rain. Combined play was , almost impossible and defence proved so much easier than attack that a pointless draw was the result Earlier in the season Warrington drew at Salford with a score of 8 points, so that the honours are even between the clubs. The home team's display on Mon- day was not very convincing, and Taylor certainly let his side down at half-back by hesitation and want of judgment. It was a mistake, in my opinion, to give him the outside position. He and Brooks should have changed places. The latter's abilities were practically wasted, so that Salford had a big pull behind the scrummage. Lomas and Thomas were overplayed by the home centres and this equalised matters.

Jenkins was one of the most noticeable forwards on the field and played a rare game. Watkin started rather shakily, but improved and had several tussles with Hyam (late of Devonport). We have yet to see what the Aberavon youth can do when he gets some scoring opportunities. He is keen and plucky—two good qualities for a footlaller.

The second test match between the N.U. and the All Blacks will take place in London to-day on the Chelsea ground. There will probably be a fine crowd, as the professional game is being looked upon with interest in the metropolis. Thomas will play for the N.U. side, and G. Dickinson has also journeyed to London as first reserve three-quarter.

To-day, Warrington make their last League visit to Yorkshire, and will be compelled to tackle Bradford with a weakened team. No less than six of the Club's best known players are in the doctor's hands, viz. : Lees, Jenkins, Brooks, Cai t w right, Landor, and Hewitt. As some compensation, Harris turns out again for the "A " team. The thirteen selected to go to Bradford are : Tilley, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Jordan and Watkin, threequarters ; Lloyd and Taylor Ihalf backs; Shugars, P. Boardman, Jolley, Belton, Harmer and Jenkins, forwards. A. S. Boardman has been dropped for want of condition.

The "A " team will be at home to Leigh Rangers, and will turn out as follows : —Bramall, full back ; Tinkler, Kenyon, Forster and Harris, threequarters ; Daintith and Kay, half backs ; Naylor, Bradshaw, Holbrook, Morley, Kettle and Fairhurst, forwards.

PENKETH INSTITUT/I.—Me final of a billiard handi- cap, which is the first since the institute has been formed, was played off on Monday evening, the finalists being Mr. J. Sampson and F. Barker. After an excit- ing game J. Sampson was the winner, scoring 100,while F. Barker scored 73. There were three prizes, two given by the institute. Dr. Murray, J.P., gave the first prize which was a beautiful cue and case. The winners were as follows :—J. Sampson I,P. Barber 2, H. Goulden 3.

BIBLE CLASS.—The Penketh Wesleyan Men's Bible Class held their open service on Sunday in the chapel, the chairman being Mr. C. E. Parker, who is president of the class. Mr. Travis, of Widnes, gave a most edifying address • Mr. Robinson, of Widnes, sang two solos, and Mrs. CI E. Parker officiated at the organ.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. --- " Love Rules the World."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. --- " Love Rules the World."

The concluding performance of this drama by Mr. Sidney Rennef's Company will be given in the Royal Court Theatre this evening. " Love Rules the World "is a play which essentially appeals to the crowd, and there have consequently been good houses throughout the week. As a dramatic creation we do not consider it stands very high, and much of both the sentiment and humour is crude. The author has woven together a complicated story in which sin and wickedness have a long reign only to be finally ousted by virtue and love. There is a villain of the deepest dye, effectively impersonated by Mr. Stephen , i Langton, a convict, a clergyman, a madman, and an I adventuress. The scenes range between the "thieves i kitchen," the prison cell, the farmhouse, and the I church, so that there is infinite variety. Miss Ruth I Sheppard has the heroine's part, and succeeds in 1, winning the sympathy of the audience right from the outset. Miss Constance Medwyn makes a dashing and determined adventuress, and the virtuous but much-wronged hero finds adequate pourtrayal in the hands of Mr. Vincent W. Carlyle. A clever , study of the tender-hearted burglar, Jim Dixey, who has to pass through a phase of insanity, is given by : Mr. Sidney Rennef. Mr. Newton Peace and Miss , Nancy Mitchell evoke roars of laughter in the parts of the policeman and the housemaid. Even when ; married their capacity to amuse does not fall away, though the humour is, at times, rather broad.

div.head: "UNDER THE RED ROBE."
div.p: "UNDER THE RED ROBE."
Dramatic Society's Performances Next Week

During next week the Royal Court Theatre will be occupied by the Warrington Dramatic Society, who will present the romantic play in four acts " Under the Red Robe. This is certainly the most ambitious enterprise which the Society has undertaken,and we have reason to believe that the production will maintain the Society's best traditions. With the autocratic Cardinal Riche- lieu as the dominating figure, the play is full of dramatic incident and excitement and we should advise all Warrington playgoers to make a point of seeing it. No fewer than 45 players will be engaged in the per- formances which will lack nothing in completeness. The bulk of the scenery will be new for the occasion and the costumes will be by Messrs. L. and 11. Nathan, of London, who had charge of the dressing of the London production of the play. The rehearsals have been full of promise, and everything points to a very successful week's entertainment. The booking has also been heavy, so that substantial proceeds should be avail- able for the Warrington Infirmary Extension Fund and the Children's Summer Camp Fund'

We read of love, we read of war, Of valorous deeds and mystic lore, But then, we've read it all before, And yearn for something newer; There's nothing fresh, the world is stale, And weary as a twice-told tale. Yet, stay when coughs and colds prevail, There's Woods' Great Peppermint Cure.—Advt.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME. " qTa ,ttt
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME. " qTa ,ttt

The attraction at the Palace and Hippodrome this week has been Mr. John Tiller's Pantomime founded on the familiar story of " Dick Whittington and his Cat." The piece is full of life and fun and runs its length brightly and crisply. Sufficient of the story is. retained to hold together a number of " turns in which spirited singing and acting combined with plenty of rough-and-tumble play is rounded off by a spectacular display in the form of pretty scenery and dresses the whole forming a two hours diversion of a quite agreeable kind. The s&nes "Highgate Hill," " By the sad sea waves," and "The Gardens of the Emperor's palace," are particularly artistic and pleasing, while much of the music, which is of the usual conglomerate order, has the merit of being bright and sparkling. In the lead- ing parts of the pantomime Miss Rene Howard as " Dick Whittington " takes first place in virtue of good vocalisation, acting and picturesque appearance. " Alice," the London Alderman's pretty daughter, is also a character well personated by Miss Nellie Rodney,while Miss Lizzie Hay as the Emperor's daughter "Zulukah" fills the part most admirably. The part of " Eliza," taken by Mr. Fred Lawrenc- is one. difficult to hold in due restraint and occasionally there is some danger of the horse-play involved in it being overdone with the result of its degenerating into mere vulgarity. Still it must be admitted that Eliza's escapades contribute largely to the animation which characterises the whole of the Dick Whittington absurdity. The part of "Jack Idle " is one full of opportunities for the comedian of which Mr. Teddy Gibbs takes full advantage. Mr. Harold Wardroper as a singer is handicapped with an extremely light tenor voice, but otherwise he fills the part of the- Emperor of "Morocco" with due dignity. There are some ear-catching choruses in which the audience- heartily participate, the best being probably " She is. a lassie from Lancashire " in which Miss Lizzie Hay sings the solo part. A visit to " Dick Whittington at to-clay's matinee or evening performance is recom- mended to all who have not yet seen this pantomime.

OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Baptist Church, Golborne-street. Medical Appointments. At this Church on Sunday the Rev. E. G. Gauge. of -- London, an ex-president of the Baptist Union, was the preacher, the occasion being the church anniversary. A meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians wa! The building was full at night. In the afternoon a held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, under the presi united service was held. Mr. J. Jarman Was the dency of the Rev. T. It. Matthews. There were also chairman, and an interesting programme of music was present :—Miss Broadbent, Mrs. Wilkinson, Mrs. Simp- submitted. The speaker, the Rev. .3. F. Matthews, took son. Messrs. A. J. Jolley, J. Billinge, W. Gill, S. Davies, for his subject" Saints and Snobs." i W. Furness, W. C. Brooks, A. Brooks, J. Backhouse, W. Stanier, G. Mather W. Flannagan, R. Forshaw, M. W. Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church. , Seton, R. Bolton, C. Sutton (clerk), J. F. Awbery The preacher at this church on Sunday was the Rev.R. (master) and A. Wright (superintendent of the Cottage W.Allen,Wesleyan Chaplain to the Forces,who also gave Homes'. an address on Monday on "The romance of Christian Work in the Army and Navy." The Rev. Sidney Pitt,who presided,in his opening remarks said that i%lr. Allen had Spent forty years of his life amongst soliders. There was no man living to whom Methodist soldiers owed so much as to Mr. Allen. Mr. Allen, in the course of his address said, there was a constant stream of young men joining the ranks, many of whom were unaccustomed to town life and there was a grand opportunity for missionary work among them. He had visited Orford Barracks during his visit and he had a most interestiug interview with the commanding officer. He went into the library where he saw a list of the men on the wall who were killed in that terrible South African war and amongst whom he recognized the name of a sergeant who had been converted and who Proved a Dower for good among the men in Egypt and India. That man came on the reserve strength and was doing good work where he lived in Lancashire When, with only two days of his reserve time to expire, be was called up for active service. He also went into the Army Temperance room where be saw the corporal- in-charge who told him that out of seventeen men who had just been drafted sixteen were teetotallers. God ,slid not "cut" a man because be drank, but tried to save aim, and we must do that as well. Mr. Allen gave some interesting reminiscences and showed that much good was being done among the recruits by the Wesleyan Church. Holy Trinity Church. . Special services were held at this Church on Sunday, in aid of the fund for repairing the fabric of the south ,alee of the church and rebuilding the vestry. The hdishop of Liverpool occupied the pulpit in the morning Whilst in the evening the preacher was the Hey. Horace Gray, master of the Boteler Grammar School. In the morning the Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Chavasse) took for his text "They brought Him to Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord," St. Luke 11, 22. That day he said was Purification Sunday. At our birth we were presented to the Lord, whilst at our confirma- tion we presented ourselves to the Lord. Whether we Were in our homer, place of business, in the society in Which we mixed or anywhere else we must think of the One who made us. We were Christ's witnesses, servants and branches and whatever Christ wished us to do we must do it, and at the last day we would have to give an account of our doings and sayings.. At the evening service the Rev. Horace Gray took for his text " And all bare Him witness and wondered at the gracious words that proceeded out of His mouth " St. Luke iv. 22. That day, he said, was the first occasion on which he was privileged to address a Warrington congregation. Referring to the text he asked why did the people wonder at the gracious Words that proceeded out of our Lord's mouth? It was because of their power and because nobody ever spoke aS the Lord spoke., We must all, he continued, examine our words and think what we were about to say because Words once uttered could not be recalled. The collections throughout the day amounted to £3O Which is very satisfactory.

Dr. Sykes says :—" Briefly the indications of experiments and observation are that the healthiness of the dwellings of this country increases in propor- tion to the amount of daylight and sunlight admitted." We want to turn our faces towards the light both in connection with our lives and our houses. Long unbroken rows of houses are bad ; the areas both in front and back are, in still conditions of the atmos- phere, like wells in which the stagnant air becxnes vitiated. BACK-YARDS. The little walled-in back-yards which are such a common feature in the construction of Warrington houses, are open to grave objection, although I admit it is difficult in town conditions to see how they can be done without. But in all the model dwellings I have lately seen these bad air traps have been crone away with, a pleasant outlook has been gained, and still the requisite privacy has been attained. In addition to the prevention of free air circulation, the room that looks into those dreary back-yards is, as a rule, the living room in which at any rate the house- wife has to spend the bulk of her time. If there is a person on earth who deserves our sympathy it is the working man's wife, who has to spend the greater part of her life in a room which has for its outlo two dirty walls, a grimy gate, an ashpit, and a closet. Is it any wonder that the natural craving for variety, for something to break the dreary monotony, should seek expression and too often find it in the most handy place, the public-house? PLANT LIFE IN TOWNS. A few months back in visiting some of the slum property in Warrington I found one solitary house brightened with what ought to be flowering geraniums. Three sickly specimens decked the window. The sun had made efforts to penetrate through the clouds of smoke which adorn the town and to dodge round a corner that it might kiss these plants into flower, and the plants themselves had done their best by stretch- ing themselves sideways towards the sunshine, but sad to say the two had never met and the life of these plants, like many human lives, was incomplete and its purpose unfulfilled. The atmospheric impurities which destroy the I health of the plants cannot fail injuriously to affect the health of the human beings who live in the district. Trees and plants are important factors in contributing to the healthiness of a town since they tend to restore the balance to the composition of the llatmosphere by absorbing gaseous impurities and I returning health-giving oxygen. This is specially so in the daylight. In bedrooms plants are objection- able. But house plants cannot do a great deal; what . we want in our towns is to break up the building areas with open spaces in which we can introduce as much plant life as possible.
